utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please, my name is Grant Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we have the appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel is my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, a professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour. My name is Zeljko Olujic, attorney from Croatia. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. My co-counsel is Michael Greaves, an attorney from England.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. My co-counsel is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am John Ackerman, I appear here this morning with Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As you would recollect, the programme for this morning has been in a flux. We are not too sure of what happened but I have just been informed that the witness intended to be called this morning has not appeared so we appear to have -- we will carry on with the argument as we intended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. The Prosecution will not be calling this witness. We wanted him to authenticate a particular document which he is unable to do so we cannot take the matter any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To follow the sequence which we want to adopt here, we would like to start with the motion by the Prosecution of 8th July. It is on the production of a handwriting sample. Could we have the argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours please. Your Honours, the Prosecution, as you know, has filed a written motion in relation to this matter which originally was raised by Ms. McHenry when she sought to produce a document during the course of the evidence of a witness. Your Honours, the issues that are covered in the written motion deal with three main points; firstly the question of admissibility generally, and in particular admissibility of documents; and secondly, in relation to this specific motion the admissibility of the letter that Ms. McHenry sought to tender; and finally, the question of the Chamber's power to order an accused person to provide a handwriting sample. To some extent, to a large extent, your Honour, the first issue relating to admissibility will also -- the submissions I make will also, to a large extent, be similar to the submissions that I would make in relation to the documents that were seized by the Austrian police. There are other issues obviously that arise in relation to those documents seized by the Austrian police, but the question of admissibility, the matters of law that I will touch upon will, to some extent, go to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please, I would like you to separate the arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Certainly I will do that, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are not taking the two motions together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand that, your Honour. I do understand. Your Honours, in relation to the question of the direction to the accused person to provide a handwriting sample, I will rely largely upon what has been set out in the written motion, but should there be matters that arise that your Honours would seek assistance upon in that, I have asked my colleague Ms. McHenry to research that area and hopefully she may be able to assist your Honours on any issues arising in relation to that, but by a large, we will rely upon what we say in the written motion itself. Your Honours, in our submission, the common law in relation to the admissibility of documents, and indeed the admissibility of evidence generally in proceedings before this Tribunal is by and large a very inappropriate and unsatisfactory vehicle by which to seek to -- upon which to rely when seeking to tender documents. I will seek to expand upon that later in terms of why I say the common law is very unsatisfactory in this regard, but I say this at the outset; that the strict common law as it would be applied in common law countries has, in our submission, been significantly modified by those common law countries, especially when it comes to the tendering of documents. We can see in an examination, if your Honours please, of the various jurisdictions around the world that substantial modification has taken place in terms of business records, with creating statutory exceptions to the hearsay principle, with dealing with public documents, and matters of that sort. Indeed, in Australia, and I do not quote that simply because I come from there, but because I think it is illustrative of the whole issue of admissibility when it comes to documents, in the High Court of that country the whole question of the common law has been commented upon by the bench from time to time, particularly in relation to hearsay, and found to be unsatisfactory. As a consequence of that, in the Evidence Act of 1995, there was substantial and significant modification in the law that relates to the admissibility of documents, such that I think it is fair to say that common law principles no longer have any significant application; and indeed, section 51 of the Evidence Act 1995 particularly provides that the principles and rules of the common law that relates to the means of proving the contents of documents are abolished. Why is that so, your Honours? In my submission, the reason for that is that with the development of modern communication, with much greater reliance on written material, and the fact that, in a normal general everyday community, we place reliance upon documents to a much greater extent, perhaps, than we did in the past when the common law was conceived, and it is somewhat artificial, in my submission, to then say, when it comes to a court dealing with documents, that it has to take a much stricter approach than that which is acceptable in the ordinary community for all sorts of decisions that are there made. I deal with this on the issue of admissibility. Of course, a document that is admitted into evidence may prima facie appear to be reliable, may prima facie be relevant and acceptable; subsequently, when compared with other pieces of evidence, it may be found to be unreliable. These are issues of weight. In my submission, the modern tendency in many jurisdictions is to move away from the issue of blocking documents from being admitted at the outset, but more to rely upon the court and the finders of fact to receive the evidence, to evaluate it, to consider it, and if the court comes to a conclusion that it is inherently unreliable, or that it does not prove the facts, or that it is irrelevant, at that stage to then say "the court will not rely on this document", and even to go so far, perhaps, to exclude it at that stage. This Tribunal, your Honours, operates in the environment of international law. In operating in that environment, there are no legislatures that one can go to in order to receive modification or modernisation, as it were, of the law. It is also very difficult for this Tribunal to pick up and apply statutory variations, for example in the common law, and apply those statutory variations. The consequence of this is that when the common law is modernised, if I can call it that, this Tribunal to some extent, if it were locked into applying a particular brand of law, if I can call it that, could not pick up those modifications. The Tribunal would be in fact locked in to a type of law, for example the common law, as it was originally conceived, and would have to disregard modern changes in the community which would make it sensible to perhaps not apply old principles of law as they were originally conceived. So I submit, your Honours, that it is for this reason that I would urge your Honours to be slow to simply say a particular type of law, whether it be common law or civil law, is the one that we should pick up and apply, but I say this particularly so with the common law. The reason I say it is particularly the case with common law is because one really does need to look at the basis, at the historical basis of which this evolved. It evolved in an environment where the finders of fact were juries. It evolved in an environment where the finders of fact were not trained in the law. It was evolved in an environment where the finders of fact did genuinely lack the ability to be able to sift through the evidence and determine complicated questions of relevance, of reliability, and so therefore, in my submission, the procedure evolved that before the jury was given this complicated task, before it was expected to give this complicated task, and their task is complicated enough as it is, the judge, the presiding judge, the trial judge, would act as a filter, as it were, and would examine it, examine the documents that the parties were seeking to tender. Upon that examination a primary filtering process would occur, and so that this burdensome task, which was by and large considered to be beyond the jury, was relieved from the jury and rested upon the shoulders of the trial judge who had the training and skill to deal with these questions. So it is, your Honours, that the voir dire process emerged. At a voir dire, as your Honours know, the issues of admissibility do not arise. One does not object to the admissibility of the document before the judge. Clearly the trial judge must see the document, and upon an examination of the document the trial judge makes the decision. What he decides is either "yes, this is a document that is (a) sufficiently reliable or (b) it is relevant or (c) it has probative value and that that probative value is not outweighed by any prejudicial effect that it may have". It is after the trial judge makes these determinations that the document then passes to the tribunal of fact, namely the jury. Of course, we do not have that here. It does not happen here, because your Honours are the tribunal of law and the tribunal of fact. In my submission, your Honours, it is absolute nonsense to suggest that you should not see the material in order to make a determination of it. It is absolute nonsense to suggest that it should not be admitted to you in the same way as it may be admitted to a trial judge at a voir dire in order for you to make a decision. Of course you must see it, otherwise you are left in a total vacuum. You have arguments from one side of the courtroom and arguments from the other side of the courtroom, but you are left there trying to determine the issue without any reference or proper and detailed examination of the document itself. Of course, some documents may be so totally irrelevant that the decision becomes very simple, it becomes excluded within seconds because of that. The document may be so inherently unreliable that the decision may also be easy too. So the whole issue of admissibility may be very quickly disposed. But in my submission, your Honours, the test for admissibility should, having regard to the fact that you perform both tasks, should be so low that it is only in the most extreme circumstance, such as total irrelevance, total unreliability, that your Honours should exclude it. Your Honours can exclude a document at any stage in the proceedings. A document that comes in at this stage might -- you may think, "how could this be relevant? How could this assist the Prosecution case? How could it assist the Defence case?" You might think that, you might ask that. But something might happen later on in the trial which raises its level of reliability, which raises its level of relevance to the point where it then changes its face significantly. It is similar, and there is not much difference, in my submission, your Honours, to oral testimony. Why is oral testimony that much different? The witness comes along, enters the witness box, and gives a version of the facts. Upon hearing those facts, your Honours may say, "I am not sure that we can accept that, having regard to what we know", but it is not ruled inadmissable as such, except in extreme circumstances. Generally the evidence comes in. Alternatively, a witness may come along and give a very credible story, a totally believable story, a story which you accept, and then something may happen later in the trial which convinces you that that evidence cannot be relied upon. The decision that your Honours make is not based on whether or not he should say anything at all and whether there should be some means by which this evidence can be excluded before he opens his mouth; not at all. The witness gives the testimony, and then your Honours compare it with other pieces of evidence, but at the end of the day you may say, "we disregard that evidence. We do not accept it. We do not rely on it". You may go further, you might say "we think the witness was not truthful". But it is not dealt with at an admissibility stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What you are suggesting is first determine the probative value and then hold whether it is admissible or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am submitting, your Honours, that the document should go to your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Determine the value and then determine whether it is admissible or not. Is that not just putting it the other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In my submission, your Honour, it is no different to what happens in a voir dire. Your Honours receive the document as a trial judge and you make the assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is a special case. It is not a normal -- if you look through our Rule 89 of our rules of evidence and procedure, it sums up all the various systems. In fact, it tells you what to do when none of the matters before you are covered under this rule. It tells you the types of evidence that should be admissible. It talks about relevance, it talks about probative value. Those are the indicia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not trying to move away from those indicia at all, your Honours. What I am saying is I am arguing the basis upon which they should be interpreted, not in any way am I suggesting that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: As a general rule, general principle, not in specific cases. The burden is different, because there might be cases where there is a burden on the Prosecution to ensure that somebody else has done a particular thing. It is only when you have shown that the burden will shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I really was not speaking of shifting burdens, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is all related to the evidence and probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The point I was trying to make, your Honours, is this: there is very good reason in the common law why the barrier, as it were, to admissibility may be higher or is higher. There is no question about it, it is higher. That is because of the structure that one is dealing with there. An example I might give, your Honours, is that in common law countries when tribunals are created, or where there are judge alone trials, it is often the case that the statutory provisions that deal with these tribunals, who are performing a task not dissimilar to what your Honours are performing, it is specifically provided for that, for example, the ordinary rules of admissibility at common law are not to apply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: There are so many national systems, legal systems which operate the same way as we do here. The judge is one of fact and law. They have their own rules, almost identical to what we have in these rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I apprehend that it will be urged upon you that the standards and principles that apply should be those that apply according to the traditional common law of England. If that is what is urged upon you -- this is the basis of my argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Our rules do not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is what I am trying to counter in my submission, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought in the common law there were three stages as far as documentary evidence was concerned. First it had to be relevant, then admissibility had to be considered, and then probative value had to be taken into account. You are saying that first consider what is its probative value, and then decide whether it is admissible or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was not saying that, your Honour. If that was what I appeared to convey, I am sorry, I did not mean that. I am not saying that. I am saying that the documents should be admissible and that the barrier should be low, and the reason why it should be low is because your Honours have the skill and ability not to be affected by material that you may be presented with which you ultimately reject on the basis of relevance, probative value or reliability. It is very hard, and it has always struck me as being very hard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My difficulty with your argument is that you are proceeding from the point of view of a national system instead of proceeding from the point of view of our own rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am hoping to get to that, your Honour, because I am at the moment endeavouring to persuade you not to place reliance upon the common law. That is the first branch of my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It should be the other way round. You should tell us why from our rules we should proceed the way you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I promise I will come to that, your Honours. If your Honours will permit me, I do wish to go through the various stages, because it is very natural, it is very natural if we are trained in a particular jurisdiction for us to automatically almost go back to the basis of our training and say, "that does not fit, that is not right", and we make definitive decisions based on the fact that that is the way we understand it to be correct. It is difficult when you come into this jurisdiction to say, "no, that is not the way you approach it at all. There are good reasons why you do not approach it that way". I will move on, your Honours, but the point that I did want to emphasise is that the common law is probably the least helpful system that your Honours can turn to for guidance in this area, and I emphasise again that not only is it the least helpful in this jurisdiction, even in common law jurisdictions, it is being found that the traditional common law is not helpful either and is being changed. Your Honours will be well aware that in large fraud cases, where people are dealing with thousands and thousands of documents and the cases go for many months, that the documents are admitted de bene esse and it is only at the end of the day the final determination is made because there is an interlinking between them. You really cannot tell just how reliable this document is, just how relevant or probative this document is until you have gone through that process of examining the totality of the material. Even at common law, the common law itself is evolving away from strict rigid principles with such procedures as admissibility de bene esse. So, your Honours, I will move from the common law to the civil law, and I will say that it does not help much either, except that a totally different approach is taken, and indeed, an approach much closer to what, in my submission, should be applied in this jurisdiction. Under the civil law codes, of course, admissibility itself does not become a major issue. There are reasons for that. One of the reasons, your Honours, is the fact that there is an investigating judge for example. Investigating judges deal with these questions often before the trial, and sets up the dossier containing the material. So it is a very different process to what we have here which blends the adversarial with perhaps civil, but basically it is an international jurisdiction which is different. So for example in most jurisdictions, and I could take your Honours to them, but I apprehend that it may not assist much if I do, but if I can generally summarise it, the emphasis is not on admissibility alone. There are occasions, I understand, I am no -- I profess to be no expert in this, but there are occasions where documents are not put in and are excluded, but by and large the emphasis is on weight and not on admissibility. The documents tend to be received and once they are received it is then at that stage that the totality of the evidence is considered. Your Honours, neither common law nor civil law helps us much on this question, and indeed, I found it interesting to see the remarks of Judge Jorda recently in the Blaskic case when he almost in frustration was saying that this contest between civil law and common law was of little help to anybody, and that really the whole issue should be looked at on the basis, as your Honours put, of the Rules of the Tribunal and indeed, questions of admissibility as have at least been examined to some extent in the international law jurisdiction. I am searching, your Honours, for His Honour Judge Jorda's comments. I cannot find them. If I can, I will come back to them, because it is a very short passage and very instructive, in my view, of this problem. Turning, your Honours, to international law, as your Honours are aware, the international law, the most active area of international law has not been in the criminal jurisdiction. The most active area has been in disputes between states or even, at best, quasi judicial jurisdictions. That is apart from Nuremberg. I do not think that in my submission one should just ignore the international law in its other manifestations, and simply say that only where international law has spoken in a criminal law jurisdiction, that is the only basis that the Tribunal should be concerned about. In my submission, it is appropriate to look at what happens, for example, in the International Court of Justice in the inter-American system, in the European system and in the International Court of Arbitration, and so forth. Before I move on into that part of my submission, I have now found the comment that His Honour Judge Jorda made in the Blaskic case. He said, on 25th June 1997, page 86 of their transcript: "I think what separates us is a conceptual problem and a legal culture. We cannot throughout this trial keep opposing one system against the other. As I said to you yesterday, the Tribunal guarantees an equitable just trial for the accused, and also allows the Prosecution to prove what is charged." In my submission, that is an expression of the concern about trying to deal with these issues on that basis. Certainly there is some assistance that can from time to time be obtained from looking at common law, looking at civil law. As your Honours know you are not bound by the common law, your Honours are not bound by the civil law. Your Honours are probably not bound by international law, and your Honours are probably not bound by decisions of other chambers in this Tribunal, but if there was to be a hierarchy of persuasive value, if I might call it that, on my submission, the lowest persuasive source of law on this issue, and I do emphasise on this issue, is the common law; the next up the ladder would be the civil law; then in my submission one would look to international law in the civil jurisdiction; and then what little there is in international law in the criminal jurisdiction; and then rise to decisions of your brothers or sisters in this Tribunal, and ultimately one would look to what has fallen from the Appeal Court of this Tribunal. In my submission, that is the appropriate line of authority to assist your Honours, and I emphasise on this point. Sometimes it may change, but essentially by and large, that in my submission is the source of authoritative reference which is open to your Honours. In the International Court of Justice, your Honours, the evidence is rarely excluded. States are encouraged to put before the court as much material as they consider is useful for the presentation of their case. In practice, while the court would place few restrictions on the rights of parties to produce whatever evidence they see fit, it has only rarely on occasions exercised discretionary authority to refuse or accept evidence that is offered. So by and large there is a very low level or low level test of admissibility before the International Court. The Tribunal established under the Inter-American Convention on Human Rights, which was by the American Human Rights Commission in proceedings before the Inter-American Commission and the Inter-American court, interested parties may offer all pertinent verbal and written information in order to clarify the acts under consideration. Again there is not a criminal jurisdiction as such. In proceedings before the International Court of Arbitration, the court shall hear all evidence that is relevant to the particular dispute at hand. Indeed, traditionally evidence is seldom excluded in international arbitration proceedings. Turning now, your Honours, to Nuremberg. In my submission the Nuremberg principles are in terms of historic and probative value, probably the best source that your Honours can go to outside of decisions of this Tribunal. In the Nuremberg trials it was emphasised that the trials were of international character. The Tribunal emphasised that they were not bound by technical rules of evidence as recognised in any jurisdiction, in the case that I am looking at, in the case of the United States or of any other country. The Tribunal tried cases and there were no juries. The main test of admissibility of evidence was established by the requirement that the tribunals must admit any evidence which they deemed to have probative value. Your Honours, Article 7 provided that evidence would be admissible if it appears to the Tribunal to contain information of probative value relating to the charges, and the types of evidence contemplated as being admissible before that Tribunal, under that test, were affidavits, depositions, interrogations and other statements; diaries, letters, the records of findings, statements and judgments of the military tribunals and the reviewing and confirming authorities of any of the United Nations and so on and so on. I will not trouble your Honour by reading through it in detail, but indeed it was very expansive. Your Honours, there are a number of examples that one can turn to in relation to Nuremberg. I will say more on captured German documents and so forth and how they were dealt with -- I apprehend I might say so at a later stage, but for example, the sorts of documents that were admitted in Nuremberg included, over objection, included such things as a photostatic copy of an unsigned carbon copy of a memorandum listing the membership and positions of the defendant Alfred Krupp Von Bohlem in more than 30 enterprises and organisations. The memorandum had been found on the files of the defendant at the headquarters of Krupp, a company in Essen in Germany. The document was offered on the first day of the Prosecution presentation of evidence. The Defence objected to its admission on the grounds that it bore no signature, and that no evidence had been submitted as to the author or where it had come from. After discussion, the Tribunal admitted the evidence, the exhibit as evidence, stating that any objection went rather to weight than to admissibility of the document. There are other cases and other documents which I could refer your Honours to and will do when dealing specifically with the other motion. So your Honours, in my submission, you can see that from Nuremberg there is a very low barrier to cross when it comes to admissibility; always preserving the right of the Tribunal to subsequently reject the material on the basis of its inadmissibility because it lacks probative value, it is either unreliable or it is irrelevant. Your Honours, if I may, the next level up the ladder, if I can call it that, of authority which may have been of assistance to you is decisions of this Tribunal. Regrettably, at this stage, there are only a few of those, but indeed there are some decisions. Primarily, the decisions come from the Tadic case, but in the Tadic case, the Trial Chamber drafted a standard of admissibility that promotes the spirit of the statute while following the letters of the rules of procedure and evidence. The tryers of fact and law in those proceedings, it was acknowledged that they were not juries but professional judges, who by virtue of their training and experience had the ability to hear the context in which the evidence was obtaining and to accord it its appropriate weight. In the Tadic decision in the Defence motion on hearsay the court said that some component of reliability was required. In our submission, the component of reliability standard is significantly lower than what is traditionally understood as being the standard that has been applied in common law jurisdictions in the traditional sense. Your Honours, there are a number of times during the Tadic case when material was sought to be tendered which the Defence argued was either unreliable or should have been excluded, and time and time again there was debate on this issue, and these arguments led to the motion that was filed upon which the decision was made. But I think it is instructive, if your Honours will bear with me, to perhaps take you to some instances of it, because it is easy to speak of these things in general terms, but when one sees it in the context of what actually occurred and to see how that court dealt with it, it may be of some assistance to your Honours. I again emphasise that none of what happened, especially during the course of the trial, has any binding effect upon your Honours at all. I am not suggesting it is binding, I am just suggesting it may be of assistance to your Honours. One example, your Honour: there was Witness Q whose evidence was taken on 11th June in 1996. The witness was testifying, and he said at line 12 on page 1496 of the transcript in the Tadic case, and I will quote, if I may, what the witness actually was saying at the time. The witness said: "The story that the guards who were down there told us was more or less as follows. As they were sitting at that guarding post near the church", and then it goes on. Mr. Kay for the Defence immediately rose to his feet, raised an objection. Mr. Kay said he objected to it and he said: "It is an important matter because it is concerned with hearsay. We are dealing now with an account given to this witness by other people making an allegation against the defendant Tadic. There are levels of hearsay that perhaps the court might well accept and admission in evidence to enable the flow of proceedings and because we are now bound by the usual form of rules, but our submission is that there comes a stage when evidence is important relating to the determination of issues in this case, when there must be some security for the Defence as to the substantial prejudice to be caused by using hearsay from other people. We are not now for the first time dealing with perhaps evidence that directly concerns allegations within the indictment against the defendant. The Prosecution have chosen to rely upon evidence through this witness, that is given by him, because he was told by others as to what took place. This, as the court will appreciate, is a matter of great concern to us." I will not trouble your Honours with the response by the Prosecution to that. Mr. Tieger was arguing. But your Honours, I will take you to what the presiding judge said at line 14, page 1497. She said: "We have said before, I suppose, that we do not have a hearsay rule. For your information it might be helpful to you lawyers, I do not think that I am speaking out of school and I ask my fellow judges to correct me if I am wrong; as you know the judges drafted these rules and in the drafting process there was much discussion about the evidence rules, and we have ten rules of evidence. I come from a jurisdiction where hearsay is a factor in trials. Judge Stephen and Judge Vohrah also come from a system where hearsay is a factor in trials. In my system, we have 24 or 28 exceptions to hearsay, so that although hearsay is not admissible, it becomes admissible, even though it is hearsay, if it fits within these exceptions. I do not know about Judge Vohrah or Judge Stephen. "The whole point though of the exceptions relates to our system in that evidence regarding statements that are made other than while the declarer is testifying by the court comes in if the court considers it is reliable if it is probative. So that our rule, even though the rule does not specifically deal with hearsay, we have this probative requirement so that in drafting the rules we will admit evidence that has probative value, probative meaning tending to support the fact for which it is admitted. During our discussions, judges expressed different views about how evidence should come in. We have looked at those views expressed, particularly by us three judges, so I will overrule your objection, and I am overruling it again, because we are a special Tribunal, and we have ten rules of evidence. We are focusing on probative value." Your Honours, there are numerous instances of this throughout the case. The objections were raised from time to time by the Defence, but in, if I can remember, all instances when it was a hearsay objection -- and hearsay is relevant because obviously one of the factors about a document is that it is a form of hearsay. It is not the declarer, not the person who wrote it who comes to testify, it is hearsay. So underlying objections to a document is that factor. I could take your Honours to other such examples because they are numerous indeed. It worked both sides. At one stage, I might say, we had the temerity to object to a Defence exhibit on a similar basis. Her Honour was more swift in dealing with us, I might add, she said she did not want to hear our objection. Your Honours, this is the basis in my submission that these documents should be admitted. Your Honours are dealing in a very special jurisdiction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which document are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As a matter of general principle, but I am dealing with the one document, if your Honour pleases. That is the basis of this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which document is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is a letter. Ms. McHenry sought to tender the letter -- I do not know whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I know where you are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: A letter written by Pavo Mucic to one of the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Allegedly written by.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, which we say contains issues of liability, which we say is relevant, and which we say has probative value. Ms. McHenry addressed you at the time on those issues. I can take your Honours back over it again if that would assist, but in my submission clearly that is the case with respect to this document. The problem related to admissibility, because the author had not been produced, the person that wrote the document had not and could not be produced in our submission, because it is our submission that it was written by Mr. Mucic. So in our submission, your Honours, this document satisfied all criteria and should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Are you abandoning the other arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honours. I thought I preserved all my arguments --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you still have an obstacle. You still have to prove it is written by him. If you can prove it is written by him, it will be admissible, without all that argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not want to have to go back over those issues again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But it has to be proved first it is written by him. Then, of course, it will be admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, in our submission we prove it to the standard of admissibility based on the contents of the document. We do it on the basis that it is written by a person who calls himself Pavo, and Pavo is a person who -- excuse me (Pause). I have been given something which has been reduced so I can read it out: "The letter contains a number of components that indicate its reliability and authenticity as a document written by the defendant Mucic. The letter was hand delivered" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not need to read the written answers. I know the written submissions contain a lot of internal evidence which you could so determine, but my anxiety is you suggested applying Rule 54 and the handwriting sample -- if you are abandoning it, you can do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not abandoning it, that is the next test. That goes to weight in my submission. The issue is admissibility. What is the point of having the document analysed if it is not admitted? It seems to me, your Honour, that is putting the cart before the horse. One admits the document into evidence, and if we argue that it has weight, your Honours may quite rightly say to us, "We cannot afford this document much weight because we are not content that it is reliable. If you are asserting it is something the accused Mucic has said, we are uncomfortable about that". Your Honours could either express that or we could perceive that as a position. We would perhaps try and increase the weight of the document by obtaining handwriting samples. It was the very point I was making, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If actually you have established that, then it becomes conclusive there will be no question of discussing any other thing, if you can establish from the handwriting examination that it was written by the person alleged to have done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But my submission, your Honour, is: why does it affect its admissibility? In my submission it does not. It cannot affect admissibility. It may affect what weight you give to it, what reliance you place upon it, but surely it cannot affect admissibility. The indicia of reliability, the relevance and its probative value, it is clear the document speaks for itself, your Honours. One admits it, but if the Prosecution is content with it only being given light weight, it may not take it any further, but if the Prosecution wishes to urge your Honours to give it great weight then the Prosecution may well have to do more, but that is no different to any document, any document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is our submission. I am certainly not abandoning any aspect of it. I submit that the issue of admissibility comes first and that I have dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Usually you do not give weight to something which is not in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is true. The next question is on what basis can it be afforded greater weight and that basis -- one of the ways it can be is by having handwriting analysis. It is not the only way, but it is one way. Then one proceeds to do that if one feels that the document should be given greater weight. It may be that the Prosecution's case is that it does not mind that it is not going to be given the greatest weight, it is not the determining factor. I have heard some submissions from the Defence about proving something beyond reasonable doubt which I still fail to understand, but I accept my ignorance perhaps of this, but it seems to me that if one was putting before your Honours one document, and the Prosecution said "this proves, this document proves that the accused murdered X, beat X, was inhumane", whatever, it proves an element of the offence, then if the Prosecution had not proved it beyond reasonable doubt I think the Prosecution would have a lot of problems. But in terms of admitting the document and collectively taking them altogether and looking at them, at the totality of the evidence, it is only then, especially with documents, it is only then that you can really make the final determination. So it has to come in if the court expresses disquiet or if the Prosecution perceives it, it then may take the other steps, but your Honours, I am not abandoning anything in our motion, as I said at the outset. Ms. McHenry will assist me, should your Honours have concerns about directing handwriting samples. She has kindly researched it for me and she will take your Honours to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You do not have to take a handwriting sample. You can produce a witness who is familiar with his handwriting and he can say it is his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. There are numerous ways of doing it. Often the greatest difficulty that the Prosecution has is finding those very people who are willing to come along and testify. We inside have enough trouble getting witnesses to events to come along to testify, let alone perhaps those. There are complications in that. It is because of these very complications that different approaches have to be taken. It is because of these very complications that modifications have been made to the common law, business records provisions, traditionally saying -- indeed not only business records, ordinary records, on the other hand documents say "if the person who wrote the document is not available or is outside of the country, then there are means by which those documents can be admitted at common law".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The source from which a document comes; that, of course, has a bearing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: -- because business records and whole files, correspondence, when the document comes in, you say well fair enough, we can presume that it is a genuine document. It depends upon facts about each document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is true. Indeed, your Honour is quite right. The source of the document is very, very germane to the issue, but it is not the only issue when it comes to admissibility. It is just as germane, the location of where it was found, it is just as germane to the question of its weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I still have some difficulties. Your argument that it should be admissible, ought to be admissible on the evidence as it is, this is your argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You have made a certain allegation. Should you not establish that allegation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And indeed if we do not and your Honours are not satisfied, your Honours should reject the document. The question, your Honour, is why exclude it from being admissible? The reason why it is traditionally excluded, your Honours, is as I explained earlier. You do not want to give this to the jury. The Prosecution makes an allegation, gives it to the jury, and says "Here, this is a letter from X, and look what it does, it says 'I admit all these offences'". The courts are very careful about that, because it is pointless saying to a jury after you have shown them that, "Ladies and gentlemen, disregard that, because we have now discovered that it is not going to be evidence in these proceedings". So the common law has crafted this process to deal with it. That does not apply here. If your Honours at the end of the day say "we are not satisfied this comes from Mr. Mucic, we are not going to accept it, we do not rely on it" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: An important aspect is that Mr. Mucic has said nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That can go both ways, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: He has said nothing about the letter, so it lies entirely on you to establish what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are three stages, proof of a document, admissibility and probative value. They come in that order. If you show it has been written by him, of course, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am not sure one has to show it has been written by him first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Proof of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The document is the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That this document belongs to such and such person, or such and such person's authorship.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: For the sake of admissibility your Honour is quite right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The second stage is, is it admissible. The third step, if it is admissible, what is its value? The first step comes first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is a very low test, at that stage. At that stage, it is right at the bottom, because, your Honour, it is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is not part of a business record, this letter. This is a one time letter sent to a person supposed to be Pavo. You have to show that it is Pavo's letter and then of course the other questions of consideration will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Under the common law, your Honour is quite right. I would have to call Mr. Mucic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Not necessarily, someone who is acquainted to his handwriting, somebody who knows that this letter has been written by him. You do not have to call Mr. Mucic for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But your Honour, the best evidence rule. I am talking of traditional common law. The best evidence rule of traditional common law is you call the author.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: If it is part of a business record or some register or something like that, of course you will take it, but here you suggest an isolated document alleged to be written by him, so you have to show it is written by him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is done by its contents, what it says and the fact that it is signed by the person, the fact that it is addressed to a person that the person knows, and all of these factors go to prove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That person has also said that he is not acquainted with his handwriting. I think that was one of the questions you asked of him. The person who received it said he was not acquainted with the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But he is acquainted with the person who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The person, yes, but not even with the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours will, no doubt in your own experience, receive letters from people all the time, signed by somebody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I regularly receive letters from someone. I can say, "I have seen letters from him, this is his handwriting", but this is a one time letter, and the person who received it was not acquainted with his handwriting, so maybe those tests are not satisfied at all. If that person had said, "Yes, I am aware of his writing, I have received letters from him, I have seen him writing", fair enough, that is by itself a proof of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I be permitted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose Mr.s McHenry might be able to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: May I be permitted to give you an example, your Honours? If I receive a letter from somebody who I may not have known of before, but it speaks of things I may know of, I may know this person, and there are all these indicia that this is a general letter from a person, I might respond to that letter. I might do a number of things with that letter, but I do not immediately say "I cannot have anything to do with this because it has not been proved to me that this is a letter from X". In the ordinary way of life one goes to the contents, who it is addressed to, the relevance of it, things which may be peculiar to the knowledge of that person, all of these issues. One looks at that and one gives it an indicia of reliability. You may say, "am I prepared to give somebody 200,000 guilders based on what is said in this letter", no, I may not, I may want further proof of the authorship or things of that nature, I may, because that is the next standard, but in my submission it works in a similar way before this Tribunal. What happens is the document is received, your Honours are entitled to have your suspicions and probably quite rightly you should have about them, and then the next stage comes -- there are two stages. It is the comparison of the document with the totality of the evidence is the first stage. The second stage is other matters such as bringing along a witness who says "Mr. Pavo, I knew him very well. Yes, I would recognise his handwriting anywhere. I do, I recognise this, this is his handwriting". That is good evidence. The accused himself could perhaps do it, it is unlikely, but he could. Or alternatively, a handwriting expert might come along and say "yes, I have examined this and I have compared it with other pieces of writing and I am satisfied, yes, that this is written by the same person". There are probably other ways which I cannot think of now, but they are ways of doing it. But that does not go to admissibility, your Honours. What goes to admissibility is what the document says, in this jurisdiction, what it says on its face and is it something which one could say bears an indicia of reliability. It does, in my submission. So that should be the basis upon which it is admitted. Unless I can help your Honours with any other matters, Ms. McHenry may assist you with the handwriting aspect, otherwise your Honours may be satisfied base on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I still have some difficulties with observing Rule 89 and the specific protection made to ensure a fair trial, because this is a matter for evidence. One does not prejudice the position of the accused by admitting this. If you look at (D), you have to think of other ways of ensuring that the evidence so admitted does not affect --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the determination of what amounts to a fair trial is a matter inherently resting with your Honours. It is not, in my submission, appropriately determined by your Honours being fearful that you yourselves will be so prejudiced that you cannot disregard the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It enables exercise of a discretion to exclude if it becomes necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, the reason why you would exclude it is because of its prejudicial effect. Most evidence that the Prosecution adduces as prejudicial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you find that the nature of a document itself, if you find that it can be produced by anybody and there was no real signature other than the fact that an assumed name was used in writing it, unless you can establish something higher like its probative value, it might be difficult for anybody to accept it as authentic, as coming from the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It may indeed be difficult to give it the sort of weight that your Honours may otherwise wish to give it. In my submission, it is instructive to look at Rule 89(E). It is instructive to look at that, because in my submission, that contemplates, by the use of the word "evidence" in 89(E), that contemplates that something has come before your Honours in the course of the proceeding, that during the course of your evaluation of it throughout the trial, your Honours have some disquiet as to its reliability. So your Honours are specifically given a power to request verification. All of this contemplates that the document or whatever it is, is admitted, that it is evidence. It says "evidence".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It is not in the circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But it says, your Honour, "may request verification of the authenticity of evidence".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: "Obtained out of court".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Exactly. That is what a document is. But your Honours could, very unlikely in my submission, say "we require verification of something before it ever becomes evidence" because there would be no point, your Honours would not know about it. It is only when it becomes admitted then your Honours become concerned about it that the rules vest you with the power to require verification of its authenticity. If the Prosecution chooses to ignore that, it does it at its peril. Your Honours will then obviously either disregard it in totality or give it very, very little weight. But in my submission, paragraph (E) of 89 lends weight to my argument that it is admitted first and it is after its admission that your Honours make an assessment and then you have the power to say "we require it", and if we do not, there is two consequences made for that. Your Honours may just reject it, that one does not deal with it as an issue of admissibility. Your Honours are not going to be prejudiced by looking at the letter. I am confident that your Honours are going to afford these accused a fair trial. I am confident that your Honours are not going to say, "well, this document does not appear to us to be very reliable. Nevertheless we are going to use it as a basis for conviction, notwithstanding the fact that we are not satisfied and we do not find it reliable". Your Honours are not going to do that. Your Honours are going to discharge the duties that have befallen you and you are going to give these accused a fair trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I am drawing attention to these provisions so you might know the limitation of whatever the Prosecution has produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in my submission, your Honours, 89(A) through to (E) completely encapsulate the very submissions I have been making. Firstly, national rules do not apply, so let us not be confused by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: They will apply if it becomes necessary. They may. They are not ruled out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They cannot be binding. They may be of some value --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Technical rules, but not as rules of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Because it says: "Any rule of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "And is consonant with the spirit of the statute".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Rules of prudence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And indeed rules of prudence, your Honour, in our submission suggest that a letter written by a person who has signed it -- a letter that is received, I will put it precisely as it is -- a letter that is received by a witness in these proceedings dealing with issues that arise in these proceedings, endeavouring to befriend that witness and do other things, and I will not go into detail, doing all those matters, and signed by a person who has a nickname, which has been -- in my submission, has to have been established in these proceedings, carries a great deal of the indicia of reliability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Would we not say "ought to carry a great deal"? That as well established, that it ought to carry a great deal. Not before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am content to use your Honour's terms. They ought to, and if they ought to, they ought to be admitted, because they ought to carry it based on that. I am happy to use that term, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the right word, it should be. Until that has been established, until that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They ought to carry it, your Honour. If they ought to carry it, they ought to be admitted. There may be other issues to increase the reliability, such as authenticity, such as proving the author, which is what authenticity is, proving the author. It may be that your Honours feel that is necessary, but it is not dealt with by admissibility, because I am confident that your Honours are not going to exclude these accused from a fair trial based on that. Just as the Tadic case, the quote that I gave your Honours, we had hearsay based upon hearsay there, and the Defence were saying, "this affects us because we cannot have a fair trial". That is not true. The court can give it whatever weight it thinks is appropriate. If the court relies on it to reach a determination and it is unreliable, then yes, the court may have done that, the court may have erred, but that is not, in my submission, what occurs. The evidence comes in and then those assessments are made. Then 89(E) is an opportunity for your Honours to say to the Prosecution or the Defence, "this has not reached a level of authenticity, of reliability that satisfies us that we can either rely on it or place much weight on it". Do your Honours wish to be addressed on the question of handwriting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you are still relying on it, you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. McHenry, I think we might take a break so that you will start at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will continue with Mr.s McHenry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. I will be very brief, your Honours, and will generally rely on what is stated in our brief. Let me first just a little bit try to clarify the matter, especially because it may have been my initial request for the handwriting sample that has caused some confusion about exactly what the Prosecution is and is not arguing here. The Prosecution has not abandoned, in any way, its argument that this court has the authority to order an accused to provide a handwriting sample. I am going to briefly speak to that matter. What the Prosecution has been arguing, both initially in our brief and then here today is that the handwriting sample is not and cannot be necessary for the question of admissibility of the document. In particular, the Prosecution believes that under Rule 89 and under rulings of this court and the Tadic decision, the Prosecution does not have to prove the authenticity of a piece of evidence, be it a document or a hearsay statement or even direct evidence, in order for it to be admitted. The Prosecution has to establish that there is some indicia of reliability and in this case it would be some indicia of reliability that the document is what it purports to be, i.e. a letter from the accused Mr. Mucic. Again, I will not go over what is already in our brief, but in this case, here in addition to it being signed with the name Pavo, the author mentions specific documents known to him and the accused, he mentions specifically the statement the witness has provided, not publicly available. He gives his own address here in the Hague, and this is sufficient for it to be admitted. The Prosecution will certainly agree that this indicia of reliability is not proof in the sense of proof beyond a reasonable doubt, that this letter was written by the accused. What we argue is that such proof is not necessary or even appropriate under the Tribunal's rules that such proof cannot be required, either of the Prosecution or in similar cases such as happened yesterday with some documents which were ultimately admitted by the Defence, were ultimately admitted by your Honours at the request of the Defence. It is the case that proof beyond a reasonable doubt or close to that may be relevant to the weight, and after this document, the letter from Mr. Mucic, at such time as it has been admitted, if it is, but not until such time, the Prosecution or this Chamber may, under Rule 54 or Rule 89(E), direct the accused to provide a handwriting sample. For sake of economy, I will discuss that argument now, although we believe that this argument must come after the document has been admitted. Under Rule 54 this Chamber has the authority to order an accused to provide a handwriting sample. In particular, Rule 54 provides that this Chamber has the authority to make such orders as are necessary for the proper conduct of an investigation or trial. There are only a few things that this Court is not authorised to do under this very broad Rule 54, and in particular, this court may not compel an accused to testify against himself or to confess guilt. Your Honours, in all systems, and there has been much discussions about how different systems work and in some systems allow certain things, some systems allow it if there is a statute; some systems allow it without anything further than required, but none of these systems find that ordering an accused to provide a handwriting sample is requiring the defendant to testify against himself or guilt. The handwriting sample is a pure identification issue, and just as this court would have the authority to order an accused to provide fingerprints; to stand in a line-up, to allow his photo to be taken, because all those are identification issues, rather than compelling an accused to testify against himself or to confess guilt. Under all those examples, this court has the authority under Rule 54 and that applies also to identification issues such as handwriting. Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There is some doubt in my mind, because Rule 54 is very widely worded, but cannot be construed in a manner which affects the rights of the accused. I believe the accused has a right to remain silent. Is not when the court asks the accused to provide his handwriting sample, is that right not being violated, the right to remain silent? I am just doing a little thinking out loud.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No, your Honour. It would be the case if your Honour ordered the accused to write down what happened on a particular day; in other words if it was his own words that he is being asked -- if it was the substance of the words that your Honours were requiring the defendant to provide, but in this case he has been asked to provide certain words which will be directed to him only for the purposes of identification. In such cases, just as your Honours could, for instance, in a line-up, it is very common in many systems that the judges order the accused to stand in a line-up and that is found to be being compelled to testify against himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It is not a question of testifying against himself. The right to remain silent.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: First of all, your Honour, let me say that our statute refers to the defendant's right not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt. That is what this Tribunal's statute refers to. It is the case that in some other places an accused may have rights that are worded and in fact are broader than what this Tribunal has said. There are some that say self-incrimination, but the words of this statute, which control this Tribunal, are that the accused cannot be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt, and we believe the plain words of the statute and their plain meaning must control, and certainly there is nothing about this Tribunal's statute that violates international law in any way. In fact, as stated in our brief, there are numerous cases, including in the European Court of Human Rights, where it has been found that requiring an accused to provide things, including handwriting samples, is not a violation of the accused's fundamental rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, is it your submission that he could be compelled to produce evidence which could be used against him if he does not wish to do so?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: It is certainly the case that the Prosecution contends that the accused can be ordered by this court to provide -- to co-operate in providing identification material, for instance, just as if an accused wanted to put a paper bag over his head so that a witness could not see him, your Honours would be entitled to let the witness, if it was relevant for identification purposes, to let the witness see them. Your Honours could also require the accused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It does look like a proposition; whether the Tribunal can compel an accused person to produce evidence which could be used against him, because his right is to remain silent and allow you to prove the allegations made against him.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you want a direct answer, if I understand your question, this Chamber does have authority under the expressed words of our statute to order an accused to provide -- let me correct that. It is not under the express, but there is nothing in the statute or in international law which would prevent this court from ordering an accused to co-operate in providing identification evidence even though that evidence may be used against him. The fundamental right of the accused is to not be compelled to testify against himself. The substance of the words, he cannot be made to confess, but it is the case that an accused can be made to stand in a line-up, to allow a witness to look at him, to allow his fingerprints to be taken, to allow his photograph to be taken and to provide handwriting issues because all those are identification issues, and the core of the right of the accused is that you do not want to force someone to testify, to give words, to confess. That is the core of what the accused's right is and it is made very clear in our statute with its words. So yes, the Prosecution absolutely believes this Chamber can require an accused to provide a handwriting sample, even though it may be that that handwriting sample ultimately, after being viewed by an expert, is used as evidence against him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: May it please your Honours, I am hoping to be rather shorter than the Prosecution in addressing you this morning. Can I first of all thank Mr. Niemann for his tour de force and wide ranging trawl through the national and international jurisdictions, some of which will be familiar to us, some of which have come as interesting news. Fascinating as it is, and one must be grateful to him for the academic exercise that he went through, my submission is that there is a completely different approach that this Tribunal must take to this issue. I am going to disappoint Mr. Niemann, though not, I hope, your Honours, because I am not going to ask you to follow the common law. I am not going to ask you to follow the law of England and Wales, which is the common law, plus all the statutory legislation that has been passed over the many years. I am not going to ask you to follow Australian law; I am not going to ask you to follow the laws of the International Court of Justice. I am not going to ask you to follow the laws of the Nuremberg war crimes Tribunal. I am going to ask you to follow the laws of this Tribunal. Those laws, the rules of procedure and evidence and decided cases, are, in my respectful submission, a distillation of all the experiences of the various judicial systems which exist all around the world. That includes not just national and international jurisdictions but the experience of, for example, the Nuremberg trials. It may well be, although I did not have the privilege of being present at your Honours' deliberations about what rules to apply, it may well be that all of those jurisdictions were looked at and some parts of them found to be wanting and some parts of them found to be useful. As I say, a distillation of past experience, and one anticipates that the rules of procedure and evidence and, indeed, the decisions made under it are effectively what this Tribunal believes to be a culling of the very best features of all the systems that we have been talking about. Can I please deal with one particular issue, and that is what I respectfully submit is a cavalier approach to the burden of proof in this case and the standard of proof. Can I respectfully remind your Honours of the existence of Rule 87? I will come to what the terms of that are in a moment. My learned friend Mr. Niemann seeks to suggest to your Honours that some lesser standard of proof exists in this Tribunal. Can I very quickly say this? The Prosecution say that this letter which they allege to be written by Mr. Mucic is a letter which proves his guilt. That is what they say, and I am going to address your Honours at some length about that issue in a moment. What they say is that the letter proves his guilt. Can I remind your Honours and I will read it out so everybody, not just your Honours, knows what is said in Rule 87; so the public outside knows what is said in Rule 87. Rule 87(A): "When both parties have completed their presentation of the case, the presiding judge shall declare the hearing closed and the Trial Chamber shall deliberate in private." This is the important passage: "A finding of guilt may be reached only when a majority of the Trial Chamber is satisfied that guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt." I give a quick example of why I say the Prosecution say that this proves his guilt, and it is at page 6 of their brief, about a third of the way down, they say: "The contents of this letter are material to several important issues of this case that pertain to the guilt or innocence of the defendant Mucic." In my respectful submission, that standard of proof is one which applies to everything which the Prosecution seek to prove, and in particular to guilt. I respectfully invite your Honours to reject the Prosecution assertion that some lesser standard of proof applies to documents which they seek to prove. I would respectfully invite your Honours to reject out of hand that assertion. Your Honours may feel that the Prosecution are uneasy with the idea of having to prove things beyond reasonable doubt, and your Honours may reflect on that for a moment. It may be that they find proving things beyond reasonable doubt inconvenient. Sadly, the law is otherwise. In urging your Honours to follow the laws of this Tribunal, I come now to the Tadic decision. It is commonly referred to as the Tadic decision on hearsay, but in my respectful submission, that is actually a misnomer, because it is in fact, we submit, sound law on the admissibility of all evidence. Can I take the trouble to quote what His Honour Judge Stephen, a distinguished Australian jurist, said about this particular issue. He said at page 4 of his separate judgment in that case, this, about Rule 89(D): "It is to be noted that sub-rule (D), while it may be applicable to some instances of hearsay evidence, is by no means confined to such evidence." In my submission, that makes it plain that the submissions that the Prosecution make in relation to documentary evidence are relevant not just to this instant case that we are discussing here today but to the whole of these proceedings and beyond that, to all cases which are tried before the International Tribunal. It having such a general application, it may well be that there are other Defence counsel who would want to have something to say about the general application of the law, not just the specific matter to hand. I hope this is not going over old ground, but I think it is important that we should remind ourselves of what the Tadic decision, the so-called Tadic decision on hearsay, has to say. In my submission, it deals with Rule 89. If I can just briefly remind your Honours of the terminology of that, and again I am going to read it out. I hope that your Honours will forgive me for doing that. They are general provisions and the important ones are rules 89(C), 89(D) and 89(E). 89(E) says this: "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." 89(D): "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial." 89(E): "A Chamber may request verification of the authenticity of evidence obtained out of court." In my respectful submission, there is a four stage process which has to be gone through in relation to all evidence. There is much evidence, of course, which everybody knows is properly admissible, is properly relevant, is properly potentially probative and for which there is no basis for exclusion, and I suspect nine tenths and more than nine tenths of all evidence is admitted into this court without objection from the Defence, or indeed one anticipates during Defence cases from the Prosecution, but there is some evidence which is challenged and the tests in my submission are these. Question number one: is the evidence which it is sought to admit reliable? If the answer to that is no, the evidence must be excluded. If the answer is yes, it is reliable, then you can go to the second stage. The next question, question two, is this: if the evidence is reliable, is it relevant? If it is not relevant, it cannot be admitted under Rule 89(C) and therefore it must be excluded, but if the answer to it is yes, it is relevant, then the next question is this: if relevant, does it bear probative value? If it has no probative value, then again, it cannot be admitted, because the rule requires your Honours to deem it to have probative value before it can be admitted. If it does have probative value, then it is potentially admissible but, and this is the fourth stage, there has to be the question: should it in any event be excluded as a result of Rule 89(D) or Rule 95? So in my submission, those are the criteria for the admissibility of evidence. As I say, most evidence gets past the first three hurdles without any problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You tend to put reliability before relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I respectfully submit it has to pass that test --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes, because if it is not reliable then in my submission it cannot even begin to attain the status of admissibility. I am going to come, if I may, to the paragraphs of the decision which I submit support that contention. Once it is admitted, it is then and only then that your Honours, as the fact finders, can determine what appropriate weight to attach to the evidence, and so, if you like, that is the fifth stage that is involved in assessment of evidence. Can I remind you of what paragraphs 15, 16 and 19 of the principal judgment in the Tadic decision say? Paragraph 15: "The Trial Chamber is bound by the rules, which implicitly require that reliability be a component of admissibility. That is, if evidence offered is unreliable, it certainly would not have probative value and would be excluded under sub-rule 89(C)." So there, your Honours, the learned judges in that decision are saying the first place that you have to go to is reliability. If you cannot get beyond reliability, it has to be excluded. It goes on: "Therefore, even without a specific rule precluding the admission of hearsay, the Trial Chamber may exclude evidence that lacks probative value because it is unreliable. Thus the focus in determining whether evidence is probative within the meaning of sub-rule 89(C) should be at a minimum that the evidence is reliable." There is a note, a footnote at that point which says this. Footnote 1 -- I wonder whether we can make sure the radio does not go off because it is terribly distracting, your Honour: "Rule 95, while concerned with the methods by which evidence is obtained also allows for its exclusion if it is unreliable." Can I remind your Honours that the decision you issued in relation to the admissibility of interviews dealt with Rule 95 in a particular way, that it is another way in which exclusion can take place, and I think your Honours referred to it as a, as it were, a residual rule encapsulating a number of ways in which exclusion can take place. Paragraph 16 of the judgment: "In evaluating the probative value of hearsay evidence, the Trial Chamber is compelled to special attention to indicia of its reliability. In reaching this determination the Trial Chamber may consider whether the statement is voluntary", that plainly relates to oral statements, "truthful and trustworthy as appropriate." Again I say the very first component is reliability. If that cannot be demonstrated, then the evidence cannot be admitted.
