Paragraph 19 says this: "Accordingly, in deciding whether or not hearsay evidence that has been objected to will be excluded, the Trial Chamber will determine whether the proffered evidence is relevant and has probative value focusing on its reliability. In doing so, the Trial Chamber will hear both the circumstances under which the evidence arose, as well as the content of the statement. The Trial Chamber may be guided by, but not bound to, hearsay exceptions generally recognised by some national legal systems; as well as the truthfulness, voluntariness and trustworthiness of the evidence as appropriate." Your Honour, those three paragraphs are the basis for which I have extrapolated the five stages that I have enumerated before you as being the process by which evidence can be admitted. I say that, and it is particularly important because reliability was the feature, I think, that His Honour Judge Jan referred to when saying "you have to prove it is his document". It was only a moment or two before his Honour intervened in that way that I had made a note to myself which read "reliability, prove it is his document". I give an example of that. The Prosecution were going to call a witness today and they have indicated that it was to deal with a particular document. They have had to withdraw him because that witness apparently cannot prove the document. In my submission, that is an admission by the Prosecution that they have to go through the very exercise that I have adumbrated to your Honours. They know it full well, we submit. So that, in our submission, is the test. We say the Prosecution has to go through the exercise in the first instance of proving that it is his document. I am going to deal with the three ways in which that might happen. The Prosecution, if they were in a position to, could prove it by handwriting samples. They say that they can prove it by the contents, and as your Honour observed, it may be possible to call somebody who knows his handwriting. I am going to deal with each of those in turn. Let me deal first of all with the question of someone who knows his writing. It is entirely right that in former days, there used to be a process by which someone who knew someone's writing could be called to give evidence. I am now going to descend into the law of England and Wales, because that is the one that I am most familiar with, but there are some comments that I make about it because it seems to me that some comments are helpful. The present law of England and Wales is this: handwriting can still be proved by the admission of the author, for example, in an interview or because he was specifically asked through his counsel to make an admission, or by any person who saw the author write it or sign the document in question. In addition, it can be proved by any witness who will at least swear that he believes the writing to be that of the party, and has either seen the person write or corresponded regularly with him, or acted upon such correspondence. The comment which is made and which I respectfully invite your Honours to take, is this: those propositions and I take this from the current edition of Archbold, business the standard textbook used in English courts, the comment is this, and my submission is that this is not just applicable to English law, but is applicable to this as a general proposition: "Many of the above cases derive from a period when communications and business documents were written by hand and literacy was infrequent. These authorities should be viewed with caution. It is submitted that identification of handwriting by a lay witness based upon a single or even a few previous observations of the act of writing, is of such poor quality that, save in exceptional circumstances, it should not be adduced. What is required is a familiarity with the party's handwriting." It then goes on to deal with the various ways in which it can be done. The practical effect of all this is this: in the 20 years that I have been at the Bar in England, I have never heard of a case where evidence has been adduced by the Crown which is someone saying "I recognise the writing" and he is called only for that purpose. The only way in which it is now done, as a matter of practice and custom, is by handwriting analysis. The reason for that is that it is now recognised that calling someone to recognise handwriting can be a most dangerous business, and of such potential poor quality as to render it an unreliable exercise. My submission is that calling someone in this court to say "I recognise the writing" would be a very unsatisfactory way to proceed, and one notes the Prosecution have not sought to call anybody who thinks they can do that, so I suspect that we will need to hear no more of that. I turn now to the issue of contents. It is said that those contents are matters which are exclusively within the knowledge of the defendant. If your Honours look at the document, that is hardly so. Each and every matter set out in that document are matters, many of them well into the public domain, but more importantly, they are matters which would be known to a large number of employees, for example, of the Office of the Prosecution. I make no accusation by doing that, and I make that absolutely plain, but it is not the case that these facts contained in this letter are exclusively within the knowledge of the defendant. There are others who could compile such a document. For those reasons, I respectfully submit to your Honours, that using the contents to say this is his document is a dangerous exercise, and one which is wholly unreliable. The third manner by which the Prosecution seek to prove the document is by inviting your Honours to have an order requiring him to provide handwriting samples. My learned friend Ms. McHenry blithely says, "Rule 54 gives you sweeping powers and you can do just as you like". It is important, in my respectful submission, for you to look and see and analyse what it is in fact the Prosecution is trying to do by getting your Honours to order a handwriting sample. Can I remind your Honours of this and I am going to re-read part of the paragraph I read out earlier, but it is important to remember what it is the Prosecution say they are trying to do. Page 6 of their written submission: "The text of defendant Mucic's letter to Witness P contains Mucic's own opinion and admissions about his conduct at the Celebici prison camp, and about specific dates of such conduct. Thus the contents of this letter are material to several important issues of this case that pertain to the guilt or innocence of the defendant Mucic. Additionally, the letter has probative value because it contains certain admissions, such as Mucic's actions in early June, and a statement that he was in charge of the Celebici camp by at least the beginning of August 1992. Thus to at least some degree, this evidence advances the enquiry at hand." Page 7: "A handwriting sample from Mucic will conclusively establish the authorship of Exhibit 155. Prosecution Exhibit 155 is relevant to the investigation and conduct of the trial, because the text of the letter is probative to the Prosecution's case. Relevancy of this letter is based on admissions by the defendant, including that he was present at the time the prisoners were moved from the 3rd March school to Celebici." We say that what the Prosecution are seeking to use this document for and it is disclosed by their submissions in writing, they wish to use it as a piece of evidence, not just to provide a piece of general evidence, but proof of specific elements of individual counts on the indictment. Those are therefore matters which are absolutely central to what must be proved in this case in order to convict the defendant, and its importance is perceived by them as no less than that. So what the Prosecution are seeking to do is use it to prove his guilt, and so they say this: "The handwriting sample will prove conclusively it is his document. The document itself will prove essential components of offences that are set out in the indictment. It will have assisted the Prosecution to prove its case against the defendant, and he will have been compelled by your Honour's order to provide that very piece of evidence." "That very piece of evidence", they perceive, will help to convict him. That is what they are asking your Honours to do. We respectfully submit that the order, if you were to make it, would have the effect of compelling the defendant to contribute to the process of him incriminating himself on counts on the indictment. We respectfully submit this, that to do so would offend against the principles which are set out in Articles 20 and 21, and indeed the rules of procedure and evidence. Again, I hope not to waste time by reading out and reminding your Honours of the text, the relevant text of those articles. Article 20(1): "The Trial Chamber shall ensure that a trial is fair and expeditious and that proceedings are conducted in accordance with the rules of procedure and evidence with full respect for the rights of the accused." It then goes on to deal with protection of victims and witnesses. Article 21(2): "In determination of charges against him, the accused shall be entitled to a fair and public hearing, subject to Article 22 of the statute." Article 21, of course, is headed "Rights of the Accused". Article 21(4)(g): "In determination of any charge against the accused pursuant to the present statute, the accused shall be entitled to the following minimum guarantees in full equality, not to be compelled to testify against himself or to confess guilt." Those articles are there in order to ensure that a fair trial is given to him and we respectfully submit one aspect of that is that no person should be forced to do any act which would contribute to incriminating himself, because that cannot properly be described as being fair. I have read out previously to your Honours part of Rule 89, but Rule 89(B) requires your Honours to do this: "The Chamber shall apply rules of evidence which will best favour a fair determination of the matter before it, and are consonant with the spirit of the statute and general principles of law." I hope it is not being arrogant to suggest that the spirit of the statute is designed to ensure a fair trial by not forcing people to do acts which incriminate themselves. An example of that, your Honours, is the series of rules that exist concerning interviews. Your Honours will recall what those rules are. Rule 42(A)(iii): "A suspect who is to be questioned by the Prosecutor shall have the following rights, of which he shall be informed by the Prosecutor prior to questioning in a language he speaks and understands." The first part is the right to be assisted by counsel, the second part deals with interpreters. Sub-rule (iii): "The right to remain silent and to be cautioned that any statement he makes may be recorded and may be used in evidence." That is a rule that is adopted by Rule 63(B) for persons who are accused. The comparison is this, and spirit of the rules is this: an interview is conducted. Why is an interview conducted? The interviewer hopes that he will get one of three things. He hopes he may get a confession, but if he does not get a confession, he hopes at least that he will get admissions, and I use that word in a different context from the word confession, admissions as to particular facts or as to particular components of offences contained in an indictment. The third thing that someone who interviews hopes to get is lies, lies which can be demonstrated by evidence to be lies, because as any Prosecutor knows, good quality lies which can be demonstrated to be lies are potent pieces of evidence. A defendant is protected against having to speak by cautions which are administered, I suspect, in every jurisdiction that can be called civilised and certainly in all the jurisdictions that are represented by counsel and your Honours in this court. The purpose of that is to give effect to the principle that people should not be forced into doing some act which incriminates themselves. That is why the rule exists concerning interviews, but it is no less important concerning other things, being forced to stand on identification parades, being forced to give handwriting samples, being forced to give blood samples, being forced to do anything which my learned friend refers to as "items of identification". People cannot be forced to incriminate themselves. This case is no different and we respectfully submit that this Tribunal should now set its face against doing anything which compels people to assist in the process of convicting themselves. I remind your Honours of Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. That is an article which finds many echos in the statute of this Tribunal. One anticipates that the persons who drafted the statute at the United Nations spent a long time looking at various similar documents. One thinks of this convention, the European Convention, but also the American convention of a similar nature, and other bill of rights acts that exist all around the world, for example, in New Zealand and Canada. Article 6 says this: "In the determination of his civil rights and obligations, or of any criminal charge against him, everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial Tribunal established by law." One could almost be reading out Articles 20 and 21 as one speaks. There are very clear similarities between those two things. I rely on the European Convention because of its international character and because it is so similar in many ways to the statute which governs this Tribunal, because your Honours may feel that the experience that has been found there is one which is readily applicable to the laws of this Tribunal. Your Honour, I have attached to the reply that I made in this case, to the back of that, a case from the European court called Funke v France. The proposition of that case is quite simple. Would your Honours give me a moment, please? (Pause). "The right to a fair trial includes the right of anyone charged with a criminal offence to remain silent and not to contribute to incriminating himself." In my respectful submission, that is something which encapsulates the spirit of our statute, and is a decision which, whilst not binding upon this court, is of immensely strong and persuasive authority. We respectfully submit that it is a proper thing for your Honours to apply and to say that however attractive at a superficial level the Prosecution's submissions may be, the fact of the matter is what they are trying to do is to get this man to provide evidence, give evidence to them which will help to convict him. That is what your Honours are being asked to do, and in my submission, it is something which your Honours should not countenance. I go on to say this: the statute provides no express power entitling you to make such an order. I anticipate that as modern scientific techniques have changed and the courts of various national jurisdictions have found a need for expert evidence, it has required primary legislation explicitly and expressly allowing police officers and courts to make such orders. There is no such primary legislation in the statute or in the rules of procedure and evidence. One must anticipate, we submit, that the framers of the rules of procedure and evidence were well aware of the various national jurisdictions which have passed primary legislation permitting such orders to be made. It is a reasonable inference that the absence of such a power is quite deliberate, and its absence is there because the Tribunal set its face against such orders. We respectfully submit that there is no power, no lawful power, whether by Rule 54 or any other rule, which permits you to force a defendant to give a sample of anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You were reading the European Convention just now, Article 6. The expression used was "contributing to incriminate himself".

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I was quoting in fact from the decision in Funke v France that is not contained within the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Contribute to incriminate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The phrase is, "Not to contribute to incriminating himself".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is much wider.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours will find that in the text of Funke v France, which is attached to my reply. I hope your Honours will find that a useful decision. Your Honours, there is one matter I pass on to, of course inviting your Honours to take into account the written submissions I have made. In proving the document, because the Defence say the Prosecution have to prove the document in the ordinary way, and I have already addressed you about the burden of proof, but part of the evidence which my learned friend Ms. McHenry sought to adduce involved somebody at the Victims and Witnesses Unit providing evidence to the Prosecution and we say that that is an essential element of proving the document, and that there is a reason why you should first of all exclude the evidence provided by the Victims and Witnesses Unit, and secondly say that because it is to be excluded they cannot prove the document in any event. The reason is this: the Victims and Witnesses Unit works for all of us. The Prosecution has to trust it and the Defence has to trust it, because all of us avail ourselves of its assistance. It must therefore be seen to be an independent organisation, an independent organisation which does not take part in the process of prosecuting people, and by providing evidence to the Prosecution, there is a danger that they will be seen to be taking part in the process of Prosecution. It is a public policy matter. If your Honours permit that evidence to be adduced, you are forever going to tarnish the reputation of the Victims and Witnesses Unit as an independent organisation, and people on this side of the Bar will cease to trust it and will cease to use it if it is seen to be being partial, and we respectfully submit that that component of reliability which is sought to be adduced from victims', witnesses', procured evidence should be excluded as a matter of public policy. That is, we submit, very important and I know that there are other Defence counsel who wish to address the court about that public policy issue, if called upon to do so. We conclude by this: we have addressed you in this way, inviting your Honours to look at what the Prosecution are actually trying to do under the veil of saying this is all about admissibility of documents. They are asking this man to contribute to incriminating himself. They are asking him to help them prove he is guilty. That is objectionable and ought to be refused. Is there any other matter upon which I can assist your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the end of your submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Those are my submissions. Impeccable timing as always.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek leave to address you for a few minutes, I think, probably no longer than ten minutes. I do not know whether you would want to do that now or wait until after we come back at 2.30, but I think the things I need to say would take about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I am not too familiar with this approach, because I think this was an objection by the team of Mucic. Are you joining in making the submissions?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Or is this a general one for all defendants?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Niemann in his arguments to you this morning went significantly beyond the issue regarding this particular document, urging you to adopt a view of evidence that had global significance, and that is what I seek to respond to. In fact, Mr. Niemann talked very little about the actual document before the court. He spoke mostly about issues of global significance regarding the evidence to be admitted in this Trial Chamber, and that is the issue to which I wish to address you for a very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: To that extent perhaps all those involved could make submissions, but generally I think we could limit it to the real issue, which is admissibility of that letter which is alleged to have been written by Pavo. So when we come back at 2.30, you will have an opportunity of replying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: With the order of the speeches, I would expect the originator of the motion to make his answer before others contribute.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please. Your Honours, there are just a couple of matters that I wish to respond to, if I may. Firstly, with respect to what Mr. Greaves said about Rule 87, it is to be seen, your Honour, that it is headed "deliberations". Clearly, in my submission, it is contemplated that the deliberations will take place at the conclusion of the presentation of the case, as the rule specifically says, "when both parties have completed their presentation, the presiding judge shall declare the hearing closed and the Trial Chamber shall deliberate in private", and then it goes on to say: "A finding of guilt may be reached only when the majority of the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the guilt has been proved beyond reasonable doubt." In my submission, your Honours, this fits entirely with the argument that I was presenting to your Honours, in the sense that if your Honours are to make a determination of the guilt or innocence of the accused, and in making that determination you place reliance upon a piece of evidence or pieces of evidence, then that evidence must satisfy you beyond a reasonable doubt before your Honours are permitted by the statute and the rules to come to that conclusion. But this, your Honours, has absolutely nothing to do with the admissibility of the document, or the admissibility of the piece of evidence at all. It is what may happen at the conclusion of the case, after the parties have completed their presentation, and it is the way -- it is instructive of the way that your Honours should then proceed to deal with the evidence, so in my submission, your Honours, to say that before it can be admitted, the Prosecution must prove it beyond reasonable doubt, and then to say that support for that proposition is to be derived from Rule 87, specifically headed as it is "deliberations", is a misconstruction of that rule. The other matter, your Honours, that I might briefly go to relate to the Funke v France case. It is to be noted, your Honours, that that decision has been considered, in a more recent case of John Murray v United Kingdom and in John Murray v United Kingdom, the same court held that the accused's right to silence is not absolute. Moreover, in circumstances which clearly -- the court held that moreover, in circumstances which clearly call for an explanation from the accused, it was decided in Murray v United Kingdom that courts may draw natural and common sense inferences from the defendant's failure to respond. If that may assist your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Which are the other discussions on general principles?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, your Honours. I want to first of all thank you for permitting me to address you for just a moment regarding these issues. I want to tell this Tribunal, this Trial Chamber, how privileged I feel to be able to appear as counsel before this International Tribunal. It is an unique experience for a lawyer to have this kind of a privilege and it is one that I appreciate a great deal. I feel privileged to be here because I believe in many ways this Tribunal is a precursor of things to come in this world, and that this Tribunal is breaking new ground with every decision that is made here. We all know that negotiations are underway for the creation of a permanent international criminal court. Our own Judge McDonald is playing a significant role, I believe, in that process. In connection with that process, of course, this court, this Tribunal and everything it does is being watched very closely by those who are considering the establishment of a permanent international criminal court. So I think that this Trial Chamber and the International Tribunal as a whole must keep very clearly in mind that what we might very well be doing here is setting a precedent for what will govern the future role of not just this Tribunal but a possible successor Tribunal with much widened jurisdiction. We must therefore be careful that the expediency of a particular situation or a particular case does not override that we keep a view on the world watching us and the world judging what it is we do in terms of human rights and the kinds of decisions we make in this court in terms of human rights. I want to talk about Rule 89. I think that is the specific rule that primarily governs this Tribunal with regard to the admission of all evidence before the Tribunal, and I think it is important that we take care in how we interpret the meaning of Rule 89. I want to give to your Honours a quote from a case that was decided several years ago by the United States Supreme court, not that it has any precedential significance at all, but I think the language is good and compelling regarding what we are doing here. In a case called Trop v Dulles, the court was considering the application of the 8th Amendment to the US constitution which deals with cruel and unusual punishment, and what its meaning was. The court said: "We must interpret the provisions of that amendment in light of the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society." The evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society. Mr. Niemann has told you this morning that he believes the most important source of law for you to consider, other than the decisions reached by other chambers and the appellate Chamber of this Tribunal, is the law that came out of the Nuremberg tribunals. I will remind your Honours that much has happened in the 50 years since Nuremberg which I think makes most of what was done at that time largely irrelevant to what we are doing here. In 1948, the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. In 1950, the European Convention of Human Rights was adopted. In the 1960s, the Warren court in the United States reached many far reaching decisions regarding the rights of accused which had impact far beyond the borders of the United States. In 1966, the United Nations adopted the international covenant on civil and political rights. In 1969, the Inter-American Convention on Human Rights was adopted. I suspect that Judge Odio Benito may have played some role in that and may have had some role in that being adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ODIO BENITO
utterances.text: I was too young at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I am glad to hear that. I hope your Honour did not hear me suggesting that your age was beyond what it appears, but it may be that you have had something to do with some of the protocols that have been dealt with since that time with regard to the Inter-American convention at least, and certainly you are well aware of it. Finally, I will just mention that what I am trying to suggest to you is there has been a worldwide growth since 50 years ago, and awareness of concern for and enforcement of human rights. In 1982, for instance, Canada adopted the charter of rights and freedoms which is very similar to the American Bill of Rights, so I do not think that this Tribunal can say the law regarding International Humanitarian Law ended with the Nuremberg Tribunal. I think it has progressed dramatically over that time and I think you must consider that progress. For instance, in 1945, when those courts were sitting, 1946 and 1947, when those courts were sitting, the death penalty existed in virtually every country in the world. It now exists in a very minor number of countries in the world. Those are the kinds of things that have happened in the last 50 years. To ignore those would be a tragic mistake. I think if this Tribunal were to adopt the suggestions of Mr. Niemann with regard to how this Tribunal should handle evidence, I think it would give a great deal of comfort to some of those who are opposing the creation of a permanent international court, permanent international criminal court. Finally, let me say this to you. Mr. Niemann has suggested to you that with regard to documents as evidence, there is no difference between a document as evidence and the testimony of a witness. I suggest to you the difference is profound and important in our legal tradition. This Tribunal has adopted what is often called the adversary system of justice. That system is designed to get at the truth, primarily through the engine of cross-examination, so that when a witness comes before you, rather than having a preliminary investigating judge deal with those kinds of issues, the witness comes before you, gives evidence and that evidence is tested, I think you have observed in the course of this trial sometimes very severely tested by cross-examination. A document cannot be cross-examined. A document brought into this courtroom cannot be put in that witness chair and cannot be asked questions regarding who it is, where it came from, who wrote it, is what is in that document true. We cannot ask the document any of those questions, so until you can consider a document, you have to accomplish basically what is accomplished with a witness by cross-examination, and that is why documents are required by the rules of this court, under Rule 89(E) to be authenticated. Authenticated means that the document is what the Prosecution claims that it is. Until the Prosecution can authenticate it, no further step can be taken with regard to that document, so I suggest to you there is a profound difference between the admission of documents and the testimony of witnesses. I think the decisions that this court is being called upon to make today with regard to both of the issues that are before you today are decisions of profound significance, not just for the defendants in this case but for this Tribunal as a whole and for perhaps matters beyond the life of this Tribunal, so I would ask you to consider these decisions very, very carefully. Thank you very much for permitting me to address you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just add one thing arising out of what my learned friend Mr. Niemann said about the case of Murray, please? It is just this, and I am sure that he meant to draw it to your attention, but no doubt forgot to do so, paragraph 49 of the decision, which says this: "The facts of the present case accordingly fall to be distinguished from those in Funke, see paragraph 41 above." The point is this: the case of Murray deals with some very specific anti-terrorist legislation which applies only in Northern Ireland and was designed to deal with professional Sinn Fein IRA terrorists. Accordingly it is a case which turns on its own particular facts and the very particular primary legislation which was the subject of that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this concludes the arguments on the first motion. We can as well proceed to the second motion, a motion which is concerned with the final determination of the issue of admissibility, filed on 8th September, affecting the Delalic case. I think this is by Residovic and her team. Can we have the arguments on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the arguments will be submitted by my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: May it please your Honours. Your Honours, I rise to make submissions on the facts and on the law in order to assist you in determining whether or not the items allegedly seized from the premises of Taubergasse 15, Door 14, and from the premises of the company INDA-Bau in Vienna Austria on 18th March 1996 should be suppressed as illegally obtained, unauthenticated and unreliable evidence. I address you on the issue, therefore, of the legality of the search and seizure at those two premises. The Defence of Zejnil Delalic claims two bases for this suppression of the allegedly seized items. The first is a motion for the exclusion of evidence, filed back on 28th May 1996, on behalf of the accused Zejnil Delalic, and further supplemented by a filing on 5th June 1996 of a preliminary motion for the exclusion of evidence, both of which were made in a timely fashion pursuant to sub-rule 73(A)(iii) relating to an application for the exclusion of evidence obtained from the accused or having belonged to him. In this Chamber's decision of October 9th 1996, decision on the motion on the exclusion and restitution of evidence and other materials seized from the accused Zejnil Delalic, her Honour Judge Gabrielle Kirk McDonald confined her decision to whether the allegedly seized items were material to the preparation of the Prosecution case. The Trial Chamber did not reach any decision regarding admissibility and suppression of the allegedly seized items; nor were any of those issues argued before this Chamber. It is submitted that the appropriate time to try the issue of suppression is at trial, as can be implied by the decision of Judge McDonald, and we submit that we are now at the appropriate stage for final determination on the issue of suppression based upon our sub-rule 73 motion. Second, and in the alternative, we submit that the circumstances which surround the seizure, the handling and the processing of the allegedly seized material offend against Article 20, paragraph 1, and Article 21, paragraph 3 of the statute of this Tribunal, as well as Rule 89(B), 89(D) and Rule 95 of our rules. We submit that these items may be suppressed on the basis of these provisions. Your Honours are familiar with these provisions and I do not propose to read them at this time. I shall return to this later in my submissions. The events which give rise to the alleged searches and seizures in Vienna on 18th March 1996 was the arrest of Mr. Zdravko Mucic in that city on that day. This same day, my client, Mr. Delalic, was arrested in Munich Germany where he lived and worked. Your Honours have heard testimony from four police officers of the Viennese police, and from one OTP investigator on this matter. The first testimony you heard, from Lieutenant Gschwendt and Officer Moerbaur, was in early June and at different times over the next three months, you heard testimony from Mr. D'Hooge, the OTP investigator, Officer Navrat and Officer Panzer. This testimony has filled over 900 pages of transcript. I shall endeavour, and I assure you I shall endeavour, to be as succinct and as clear as possible regarding the facts in this matter, but some detail is required to present to you the reasons why we submit that the allegedly seized items from Taubergasse 14 and from INDA-Bau should be suppressed. Your Honours, the Prosecution has been put to strict proof of showing both that proper procedures were followed by the police in Vienna in conducting the alleged search and seizures and that the chain of custody can be established, beginning at the premises from which the items were allegedly confiscated to their arrival at this Tribunal in The Hague. We submit that the burden of proof which the Prosecution must meet is that of beyond reasonable doubt. We find support for this proposition both in Rule 87 of our rules, and in the written decision of this Chamber on 1st September 1997, when it ruled inadmissable the statement made to the police in Vienna by the defendant Mucic, and therein at paragraph 40, we read and I quote: "It is universally accepted that the burden of proof lies on the Prosecution, the standard of proof on the Prosecution is proof beyond reasonable doubt." Before making submissions on the law, your Honours, I propose to review the evidence with you by looking primarily at two aspects of it which I submit are relevant to determining the issue of suppression. They are first the procedures followed by the police in Vienna in carrying out the searches and seizures, and second, the issue of the proof of the chain of custody from the time the allege -- the items were allegedly seized to their ultimate transfer to the Office of the Prosecutor. I propose to begin by looking at the search warrant, which was issued in connection with Taubergasse 15 and INDA-Bau. This search warrant is Prosecution Exhibit 163. This search warrant indicates that it is based on Article 139 of the Austrian code of criminal procedure. During the testimony of Lieutenant Gschwendt, your Honours heard that pursuant to Article 139 of the Austrian code, a search warrant may only be issued if a well-founded suspicion exists that either the person sought or his belongings are found to be in the premises which are the object of the search. While being cross-examined by my learned colleague Mr. Moran, Lieutenant Gschwendt told your Honours that the police had no facts to support the suspicion to have the search warrant issued. Furthermore, the testimony of officers Moerbauer and Panzer showed that the well-founded suspicion did not exist, because Zejnil Delalic was known to live in Munich and he had not been registered at apartment 14 since November 1995; that is to say five months prior to the search of those premises. It was further shown through Officer Panzer that two adults and two children, with the family name Halilhodzic were registered as living at apartment 14 in March 1996. It is submitted, your Honours, that when the facts show that Zejnil Delalic has not been living -- has not been registered as living at apartment 14 for five months, and what appears to be a family of four is registered as living in that apartment, it cannot be said that there is such grounds to issue a search warrant against Zejnil Delalic for those premises. Moreover, your Honours, in regards to the search warrant for INDA-Bau, we submit that the issuing of the search warrant for that premises under Article 139 is not well-founded. As your Honours know from the evidence, Mr. Delalic lived and worked in Munich, Germany. You also heard in the testimony of Officer Panzer that following a company search of INDA-Bau, through the public documents, the public registration on that company, the police knew that Zejnil Delalic was not and had never been a director or shareholder or in any way connected with that company. Furthermore, your Honours have heard no evidence connecting Mr. Mucic to INDA-Bau. It is submitted that, as in the case of apartment 14, there was insufficient grounds to issue a search warrant either against Mr. Delalic or against Mr. Mucic in connection with INDA-Bau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. The searches were carried out in pursuance of a warrant issued by Dr. Seda.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do we have his entire record before us, Dr. Seda, the material that was before him?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I do not believe that is in evidence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is it not premature to raise this matter at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Based on the evidence of Lieutenant Gschwendt who was involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But this search warrant was issued by a court, a competent court and we do not have the record of that court before us, so how can we say there was no ground for issuing the search warrant. We do not have the order of Dr. Seda in this regard, we do not have the material Dr. Seda had before him. Is it not premature? Why do you not wait until the entire Prosecution evidence is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Very well. To respond, based on the evidence of Lieutenant Gschwendt who was responsible, by his own admission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Merely executing a warrant issued by a court, a competent court.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I move on and I leave it to the Prosecution, who has the burden, to prove that the warrant was effectively legally issued. In addition to the problems with the search warrant, your Honours, it is submitted that the following breach and procedure under Austrian law exists in connection with apartment 14. It is submitted that the police in Vienna knowingly had Sanda Mucic, a girl of 16 years, act as a witness to the search in apartment 14 in violation of Article 142, paragraph 2. Your Honours will recall that this provision, which was reviewed with Officer Panzer at page 6591 of the transcript, states that if the owner of the premises is not present an adult member of his family should be present, failing which, a fellow lodger neighbour should be present. In all cases, we were told the witness must be an adult. Sanda Mucic signed the Niederschrift for apartment 14 as a witness to the search. The Niederschrift for apartment 14 is Exhibit D65/1. Your Honours will also recall that on the question of the age of Sanda Mucic, the document which listed the individuals registered and no longer registered as living at Taubergasse 15 was reviewed with two Prosecution witnesses. This document is marked as Defence Exhibit D62/1, a document which Officer Moerbauer admits to having prepared. Both Officer Moerbauer and Officer Panzer acknowledged, when looking at Exhibit D62/1, that Sanda Mucic, born on 27th April 1979, was only 16 years old on 18th March 1996. It is submitted that during the testimony before this Tribunal, Officer Moerbauer tried to mislead your Honours regarding the fact that he knew Sanda Mucic was 16 years old. Beginning on page 3677 of the transcript, while being cross-examined by my learned colleague Madam Residovic, the following exchange took place. Officer Moerbauer is being questioned about the presence of Sanda Mucic in apartment 10 at Taubergasse 15: "Question: At that moment, you knew that Sanda Mucic was a minor and that she was only 16? Answer: I did not note that fact because I did not go into any details about Sanda Mucic, but on the basis of her experience, her appearance, one could readily take her for 18 or 19 years of age." Your Honours, Officer Moerbauer is not to be believed in answering this question, and I say this for two reasons. First, Sanda Mucic's date of birth is indicated in the registration information, marked as 62/1, which was prepared by Moerbauer. The second reason can be found in a report which is marked as D63/1. The report is dated 14th March 1996. It is signed by officers Moerbauer and Borlak. It is a report prepared in anticipation of the events of 18th March. In the second paragraph of that report, it clearly states that the date of birth of Sanda Mucic is 27th April 1979. I hasten to add that officer Borlak was also at apartment 10, Taubergasse 15, on 18th March, along with officers Panzer and Moerbauer during the search of that premises. Your Honours, it is submitted that based on this report, both Moerbauer and Borlak knew that Sanda Mucic was only 16 years old. Finally on the question of Sanda's age, both Officer Moerbauer and Officer Panzer told your Honours that Sanda Mucic was left in the care of an adult. It is indeed submitted that this happened because they knew she was only 16 years old. There is also a question about whether or not Sanda Mucic was present during the whole time the search took place in apartment 14. Beginning at the bottom of page 3689 of the transcript, on cross-examination by Madam Residovic, Officer Moerbauer was asked about going up to apartment 14 while the alleged search was being conducted: "Question: At the time you entered the apartment of Mr. Delalic, you only had contact with your colleagues Unger and Winkelmann in that premises; is that correct? Answer: I only had contact with those two persons. Question: At that time in the apartment of Mr. Delalic, there were no third persons present; is that correct? Answer: I did not see any third person." These questions and answer indicate that Sanda Mucic was not present in apartment 14 some of the time, if she was there at all, while the alleged search took place in this premises and this is consistent, I submit, with the evidence that puts Sanda Mucic one floor down, in apartment 10, during this period on the afternoon of 18th March 1996. One must ask why, then, a 16 year old girl was knowingly selected to witness the search of apartment 14, in clear breach of the Austrian code, when other adults were available to act as witnesses in compliance with the Austrian law on 18th March 1996 at Taubergasse 15. Before leaving this point, let me add this your Honours. Aside from the reasons your Honours have just heard which show that Article 142, paragraph 2 of the Austrian code was violated, the fact that the Viennese police would knowingly have a 16 year old girl, who undoubtedly was very distraught when she came home to find her father in handcuffs and to be handed his arrest warrant to translate to him, the fact the Viennese police would have this girl witness the search is not only a clear violation of the law, but is nothing short of disgraceful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute, the provision in the Austrian law regarding the presence of witnesses is of mandatory nature or merely directory? The provision in the Austrian law that witnesses must be present, is it of a mandatory nature or only directory?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: It is mandatory and is in fact reflected in the Niederschrift where the witness to the search must sign. For now, your Honours, I put to one side submissions regarding breaches of the Austrian code of procedure and I turn to the issue of chain of custody. Your Honours will recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Before you go further, actually the provision about presence of witnesses is what should be complied with. What should be complied with after the execution of the warrant, these conditions about the presence of witnesses ought to be complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, and the Niederschrift provides for the -- the Niederschrift being the document prepared --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The Austrian provisions, which wants the police to comply with those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Is there any precedent from the Austrian jurisdiction with regard to the interpretation of this section?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, we have the testimony of a couple of police officers --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am talking about precedent, decisions given by the Austrian courts with regard to the nature of this provision, is it directory or mandatory. I just want to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question. I do not know, your Honour. I propose now to turn to the issue of chain of custody. Your Honours will recall that during the testimony of Officer Moerbauer in June, your Honours made proof of the chain of custody of the allegedly seized items a condition precedent to their admissibility. I remind the Tribunal that on Monday, 9th June, at page 3645 of the transcript, the Prosecution made an offer of proof to establish the chain of custody. I quote my learned friend Mr. Turone, who had this to say to your Honours during the testimony of Officer Moerbauer. I quote: "Your Honours have indicated already that they wish to hear from several officers who actually seized the material and then gave it to Mr. Moerbauer, but we are going to do that, but it is still the case, however, that in addition, this witness [Mr. Moerbauer] be allowed to recognise every single document he might have received from Unger, either Unger or Navrat, because he is the only person who did a specific detailed inventory of those documents. So I repeat, we will call Mr. Navrat, we will call Mr. Unger, we might even call back Mr. Moerbauer after that, in order to recognise at that time, one by one, the documents he received from Navrat and from Unger." The Prosecution said that Unger and Navrat could prove that they seized the items from number 10 and INDA-Bau respectively, and that since Moerbauer was handed the materials by Unger and Navrat, and thereafter analysed it, the chain of custody is complete. It is our submission that the Prosecution has failed to do so, either as they said they would prove it, or in any other way. Your Honours, before fully developing my submissions on the issue of chain of custody, allow me to remind your Honours briefly how and why this issue arises in this case. First, in regard to apartment 14, I direct your Honours to the Niederschrift which is Exhibit D65/1. That is the Niederschrift for apartment 14. In this Niederschrift, among the items allegedly seized from apartment 14, it is indicated that 30 video cassettes were confiscated. Let me emphasise the importance of this point in relation to the issue of chain of custody. I do so by referring your Honours to the Bericht for apartment 14, Exhibit D66/1. The Bericht is the document that follows the Niederschrift. This is the Bericht dated 18th March 1996, prepared in connection with apartment 14, the English word for Bericht is report. In this Bericht, it states that 28, not 30 video cassettes, were confiscated from apartment 14. There are two points to be made immediately in regard to this Niederschrift and this Bericht. The Niederschrift was prepared in its entirety on the premises of apartment 14. To answer your question, Judge Karibi-Whyte, it is the document prepared on the spot, on the premises, which records events such as the witnesses, items seized. The Bericht was prepared at police headquarters after the allegedly seized items returned to police headquarters. It is at this point that a discrepancy is noted concerning the allegedly seized items from apartment 14. They had changed. These documents point out the beginning of what becomes a serious problem in the chain of custody. As for INDA-Bau, allow me to make these preliminary observations. Here too, on the face of the documents, there are discrepancies between the allegedly seized items which are recorded on the premises and the documents prepared later back at police headquarters. Here too, one must begin with the Niederschrift for INDA-Bau, which is Prosecution Exhibit 165. Among the items listed as confiscated in the Niederschrift are 51 video cassettes. The Niederschrift must be compared with two reports, two Bericht, two reports, subsequently prepared at the Viennese police headquarters in relation to INDA-Bau. The first is the Bericht which is Exhibit D56/1. This Bericht was prepared by Officer Navrat on 18th March 1996, after he returned to police headquarters with the allegedly seized items from INDA-Bau. This report indicates, once again, that there are 51 video cassettes. The second relevant document to look at, at this stage, is the subsequent Bericht, which is D57/1, and this Bericht is dated 22nd April 1996, and was prepared by Bychek and Panzer. This document indicates that 54, not 51 videos were seized at INDA-Bau during the search of those premises. Your Honours, I have just reviewed for you the basis which gives rise to the issue of the chain of custody in this matter. Your Honours have seen discrepancies in regard to the allegedly seized items both from Door 14 and from INDA-Bau. I pause here to remind your Honours that during the testimony of Officer Navrat, a police officer with 18 years experience, he explained the purpose and importance of the documents prepared in connection with the search to which I have been making reference. We heard from Officer Navrat that the Niederschrift is the only document prepared on the premises during the search. By its very name, it is the record of the search. Officer Navrat confirmed that the Niederschrift is the only official document which is signed by the person concerned, or his representative, on the premises. A copy of the Niederschrift is left at the premises. The Niederschrift is thus the best proof of such things as the names of the people present, the officers who conducted the search, and the objects seized. The connection between these documents and the issue of the chain of custody is this: the Niederschrift, prepared and completed in its entirety, both at 14 and INDA-Bau, lists items which are different from the items prepared in reports later at police headquarters, and in the case of INDA-Bau, these discrepancies are noted for the first time in a report dated 22nd April 1996, more than one month after the alleged search and seizure. There is no witness, no representative of the person concerned when these reports or all other subsequent documents are prepared following the Niederschrift. It is submitted that aside from all other irregularities and illegalities associated with Door 14 and INDA-Bau, it is clear from these documents themselves that some, if not all of the items allegedly seized at 14 and INDA-Bau, change from the time that these Niederschrift are prepared on the premises to the time when these items are itemised and recorded in records or reports, Bericht, which are prepared later at police headquarters. Your Honours, with that background, I now propose to look in greater detail at the events surrounding both of these searches at 14 and at INDA-Bau. I remind your Honours of the offer of proof made by the Prosecution, namely that they would prove the chain of custody as between Unger and Moerbauer for apartment 14. The first thing to point out is that officer Unger was not called as a witness; nor was his colleague Winkelmann. According to the Niederschrift for 14, D65/1, they were the two police officers who conducted the alleged search and seizure at apartment 14. Your Honours have therefore heard no evidence from an officer who participated in the alleged search at apartment 14. The Prosecution has offered no evidence to prove even the first link in the chain for these premises. Furthermore, your Honours, as between Officer Moerbauer and Panzer, there is conflicting testimony regarding the care and control of the allegedly seized items from apartment 14, between their seizure and the return to police headquarters. I am just talking about that period between the seizure and the return to police headquarters. Both Officer Moerbauer and Officer Panzer had clear recollections of events and their accounts are quite different. Beginning on page 3549 of the transcript, during direct examination, Officer Moerbauer said that at one point during the search of apartment 14 he was requested by either Unger or Winkelmann to go up one flight to apartment 14. At that time, Officer Moerbauer was one floor below in apartment 150. On page 3549 of the transcript, Officer Moerbauer states that in apartment 14 he was shown a bag on the desk, videotapes and documents. In the apartment Officer Moerbauer says he was with his colleagues Unger and Winkelmann. Officer Moerbauer then testified that in the hallway, after the door to apartment 14 had been locked, he received the black sports bag from the officers who conducted the search, the bag in which all the allegedly seized items from 14 were placed. At page 3550, at line 24, Officer Moerbauer gave this account of having received the black sports bag after the door to apartment 14 was locked. He said and I quote: "When it was locked, the seized objects and the record, along with the keys, were handed to me." Officer Moerbauer then testified that he brought the black sports bag back to police headquarters, and at police headquarters he handed the bag back to either Unger or Winkelmann. At page 3551, beginning at line 4, Moerbauer had this to say: "Question: Did the colleagues who carried out the search in Delalic's apartment join you after the search? Answer: Yes. Question: Where did they join you? Answer: In the police headquarters in our office. Question: Was the whole seized material carried there? Answer: The seized material was brought there and the two colleagues had gone ahead, because there is a report. After a search, you have to draw up a report about it. Question: Did you personally see again in the police premises the same day the material which was seized in Delalic's apartment? Answer: Yes, I did see it. I took it along to headquarters as well. I took it to the colleagues who wrote the report, because I was waiting for the report on the search." I invite your Honours to compare Moerbauer's versions of events with the following account concerning the alleged seizure in apartment 14, which was given to this Tribunal recently by Officer Panzer, the last witness we saw. At page 6450 of the transcript, Officer Panzer said this: "Mr. Moerbauer went up to Delalic's apartment, and I went up to Delalic's apartment. They would ask, is this relevant, should this be seized or not? After the search in Delalic's apartment was over, I happened to see a gym bag there. I took that along. I put all the items seized in the apartment of Mr. Delalic in that. That bag, I took that bag to the car as well." It is said: "I think Borlak carried the things upstairs at police headquarters with me." I pause and ask your Honours to consider the difference in these two accounts with regard to the chain of custody issue. Moerbauer says he is up in apartment 14 with Unger and Winkelmann, no mention of Panzer being there. After the search, Moerbauer receives a black bag in the hall. It is given to him by one of the two police officers who conducted the search. Moerbauer says he transports the black bag back to headquarters. At headquarters, Moerbaur says he hands the bag to his colleagues who must prepare a report. Panzer says he and Moerbauer were up in 14. Panzer says at the conclusion of the search he happens to see a gym bag in the apartment. He puts the items in a gym bag. Panzer takes the bag to the car. Borlak takes the bag from the car at police headquarters upstairs. Based on this testimony, your Honours, it would appear we are talking about two sports bags. It is clear from this testimony that the black sports bag over which Moerbauer had care and control is not the same bag over which Panzer and Borlak had care and control. Furthermore, in regard to apartment 14, the evidence is clear from all accounts of all the witnesses who came to testify that none of the allegedly seized items was marked before leaving. The bags in which these things were transported was not marked and the bag was not sealed. As I have already mentioned, the evidence before you does allow you to be sure of one thing. The items were Taubergasse 15, Door 14 change from the time they are allegedly seized to the time that they are examined at police headquarters. As your Honours have already seen, a comparison of the Niederschrift, D65/1, and the report, D66/1, make that clear. We go from 30 videos in the Niederschrift to 28 in the reports. The immediate question is, are we talking about 2 less tapes, 28 different tapes or some variation thereon? In fact we are not sure whether we are even talking about the same sports bag. I hasten to add that if the most tangible items, the video, the items which are the easiest to count have changed, it is not unreasonable to say that the other items have changed as well. I wish to emphasise, your Honours, that the timeframe which we are looking at is only from the time that the allegedly seized items were taken from Door 14 until returning to police headquarters late in the afternoon on 18th March 1996 around 5.00 pm. It is submitted that there are other intervening events which occur thereafter, after 5.00 on 18th March, and which I shall discuss shortly with you which are relevant to the issue of chain of custody which again compound the problem, but before moving on let me draw your Honours' attention to one more fact one can see by merely looking at the documents. In the Niederschrift for apartment 14, that is Exhibit D65/1, in a rather short list of items allegedly seized, we find, and I repeat, 30 cassettes, one black sports bag. In the report, D66/1, not only has the number of cassettes changed from 30 to 28, there is no longer any reference to a black sports bag. The sports bag only makes a reappearance in the report on 22nd April 1996. This is a report prepared by Bychek and Panzer. Your Honours can find this April 22nd report in Prosecution Exhibit 104. 104 is the lengthy document that has been admitted, and you will find this April 22nd report for apartment 14 in the English version at page 7, the English translation page 7, or if you would prefer the stamp number is 00486348. Your Honours, I have just gone through the events surrounding the alleged search and seizure at Taubergasse 15, Door 14, and the period I have been talking about is from the time that the alleged search took place until approximately 5.00 in the afternoon, when things were back at police headquarters. I now propose to cover this same period for the alleged search and seizure at INDA-Bau, the same period, from the search until we return at police headquarters. I remind you first, your Honours, of the offer of proof made by the Prosecution in relation to the chain of custody at INDA-Bau, namely that they would prove the chain of custody as between Officer Navrat and Officer Moerbauer. Your Honours heard testimony concerning this matter from Moerbauer, Navrat and Panzer. The first account your Honours heard with regard to the continuity of evidence in relation to INDA-Bau was given by Officer Moerbauer. He testified that at about 5.00 in the afternoon, on 18th March 1996, in room 331 at police headquarters, Officer Navrat handed him a cardboard box containing documents and video cassettes from INDA-Bau. Officer Navrat testified -- when Officer Navrat testified, he gave a different account. Officer Navrat said that at police headquarters he handed the items not to Officer Moerbauer but to Officer Panzer. Not only does Officer Navrat's testimony conflict with that of Officer Moerbauer over who received the items at police headquarters, but there are other significant differences between their testimony. Officer Moerbauer has said that all videos and folders from INDA-Bau were in a cardboard box. Officer Navrat said that the folders were in a plastic bag and that the video were in a cardboard box. Officer Moerbauer said he received the cardboard box from Officer Navrat in room 331 of police headquarters. Officer Navrat said he handed the plastic bag containing the folders and the cardboard box containing tapes to Officer Panzer in room 326 of police headquarters. As for Officer Panzer's version, he confirms that he received the items from Officer Navrat, contrary to Moerbauer's account, but Officer Panzer makes no reference to a plastic bag containing folders. At page 6464, Officer Panzer says: "Mr. Navrat brought me 12 folders with various papers, newspaper cuttings were there, and there was also a box with video cassettes." Your Honours, based on the testimony of these three police officers, we are left with this: we have inconsistent testimony concerning who received the allegedly confiscated items from Officer Navrat at police headquarters. There are inconsistencies regarding the container or containers, whichever version one might accept, in which these items arrive at police headquarters, and there are inconsistencies in relation to the room in police headquarters where these items are brought. On this last point it is clear that room 331 and room 326 are different offices in police headquarters, which suggest perhaps that items allegedly coming from INDA-Bau were brought both to Moerbauer and to Panzer by Officer Navrat. There may have been two sets of items, two cardboard boxes. Who knows? As for the allegedly seized items from INDA-Bau themselves, your Honours have already heard that as between the Niederschrift and the report of 18th March, the items do not change. Officer Navrat prepared both, he signed the Niederschrift and he signed the first report on 18th March. The items do not change. The Niederschrift in question is Exhibit 165 and the report is D56/1. The Niederschrift was completed on the premises of INDA-Bau, and the report of 18th March was completed at police headquarters. On the face of this document, the list of allegedly seized items is the same. I say on the face of the documents, because during his testimony Officer Navrat said that he did not check the items from INDA-Bau when he returned to police headquarters. He relied entirely on the contents of his Niederschrift in preparing his reports. This is significant for the following reasons, I submit. As we shall see shortly, documents prepared in April 1996 in connection with INDA-Bau indicate that the allegedly seized items change. Whether they change from the time they left INDA-Bau to the time they arrived at police headquarters, or whether the items changed after arriving at police headquarters, we will never know -- we may never know. I raise this point because aside from the conflicting testimony regarding delivery of these items at police headquarters, the testimony of Officer Navrat confirms that none of the items were marked before leaving INDA-Bau. The container or containers in which they were transported was not marked, nor was the container sealed before leaving INDA-Bau. The document which records a change in the allegedly seized items from INDA-Bau is a report dated 22nd April 1996 to which I made reference earlier. This report is part of Prosecution Exhibit 104. I refer you to the English version, the English translation of Exhibit 104, page 7. It is the report prepared by Bychek and Panzer in relation to INDA-Bau. It is submitted that the date of this report, April 22nd 1996, is significant in determining the issue of the chain of custody. It is significant for this reason. So far, your Honours, we have been following the allegedly seized items from apartment 14 and from INDA-Bau, from those two premises, to police headquarters on 18th March 1996. It is submitted that your Honours have already seen evidence which raises a reasonable doubt as to the continuity of this evidence. However, once back at police headquarters, beginning on the evening of 18th March 1996, there is further evidence which in our submission compounds the problem of the chain of custody. I now propose to take your Honours through the evidence which we submit is relevant to the issue of custody, from the time the items from Door 14 and INDA-Bau arrive at police headquarters on 18th March to the preparation of these reports on 22nd April 1996, and its ultimate transfer to this court in The Hague. So far we have gone from 14 and INDA-Bau to police headquarters, 5.00 on 18th March. Now I want to go from 5.00 on 18th March to the other set of reports in April, a month later approximately, and thereafter, because they leave Vienna and end up here. It is submitted that the evidence of three Prosecution witnesses is relevant to this portion of the chain of custody in connection with the events at police headquarters on the evening of 18th March. I want to talk about the evening of 18th March. Those three witnesses are Officer Panzer, Officer Moerbauer and officer D'Hooge, the OTP investigator. Officer Panzer told this Tribunal that at about 5.00 on 18th March 1996, upon his arrival at police headquarters, he went directly to room 331, where he put the items allegedly seized from Door 10 and Door 14 at Taubergasse 15, as well as the items from INDA-Bau, in a cabinet which was in room 331. Officer Panzer testified that only he, Bychek and Moerbauer had access to room 331 and to the cabinet in that room. He says this at page 6462. Officer Panzer told your Honours that he marked the items from Door 10 in the evening of 18th March 1996 at around 8.00 pm, and that he marked the items from the other two locations, apartment 14 and INDA-Bau, on the next day, on 19th March 1996. At one point in his testimony, on page 6555, Officer Panzer said that on the evening of 18th March 1996, for the most part until Mr. Mucic was handed over, taken to jail, nine people had access to room 331: Mucic, Mr.s Supert, the German interpreter, Borlak, Moerbauer, Bychek, Gschwendt, Fammler, the legal advisor, Navrat and Panzer himself. Your Honours, it is submitted that Officer Panzer was attempting to say that room 331 and the cabinet in that room containing the allegedly seized items from all three locations was under the care and control of only a few police officers, and that only a few authorised people had access to room 331. Indeed, on cross-examination, beginning at page 6564, line 22, Officer Panzer gave the following evidence concerning the items from Door 10, which he says he put in the cabinet at around 5.00 pm on 18th March and which he removed from the cabinet to mark at approximately 8.00 pm: "Question: From the time you put these items in the cabinet until you marked these items, did they remain the whole time in the cabinet? Answer: No, they stayed in the cabinet the whole time." On page 6565, beginning at line 1, the questions and answers continue concerning alleged items from apartment 10: "Question: From 5.00, when you put them there, until you took them out to mark them, they stayed in the cabinet? Answer: All the seized items, once they were handed over, were put in the cabinet and all the items from the same locality were placed on the same shelf. Perhaps Mr. Bychek, Mr. Moerbauer and myself in the meantime took something out, had a look at it, put it back in, but they were always in there. Put it this way, I cannot really say whether they were under lock and key at absolutely all times. Question: When you were finished marking the videos and items from Door 10, you put them back in the cabinet? Answer: I put them back in the box in the back of the cabinet, yes." Then moving down to line 19 on page 6565: "Question: The other items that are in the cabinet, other than Door 10, they remain in the cabinet from the time you put them there about 5.00 on the 18th until some time the next day; is that correct? Answer: They were in the cabinet, items were always in the cabinet, put it that way." Your Honours a little later in the same cross-examination, Officer Panzer was asked if representatives from the OTP were at police headquarters on the evening of 18th March 1996. His version of events changed, both in regards to the people who had access to room 331 and in regards to the allegedly seized items. On page 6569, beginning at line 11, Officer Panzer says this: "Question: The Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, their representatives were also in room 331? Answer: People from the Tribunal looked in. As to when that was and how long they were there, I cannot say. They were not in room 331, they were rather in the room next door." Officer Panzer elaborates further on page 6570, beginning at line 5: "Question: You say that the representatives of the Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal were never in room 331; is that correct? Answer: They did come into the room, but they were staying, as it were, in the next room. That is where they were located, as it were." As for the allegedly seized material and the access of the representatives of the OTP to those items on the evening of 18th March 1996, Officer Panzer says this at page 6573: "Question: Is it not correct that in room 331, the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor were allowed to look at allegedly seized items from doors 10, 14 and INDA-Bau? Answer: That is right. Question: These items were placed on a table, on one of the times in room 331? Answer: I think they were in the next room on the table. The seized items, I took them out of the cabinet, I and Moerbauer gave it to them, they had a look at it, then I took it back and put it in the cabinet." Your Honours, I pause here for a moment. At this point in his testimony, not only has Officer Panzer seemed to recall the OTP being in room 331, when they had a look at the allegedly seized items, now he remembers taking these items out of the cabinet and in fact out of room 331 to take them to room 329 where the OTP representatives were located. Furthermore, your Honours, in answering these questions which I have just read to you, Officer Panzer was not sure when and for how long the OTP was there on the evening of 18th March 1996. That is where the testimony of Officer Moerbauer and Officer D'Hooge, the OTP investigator, is very helpful. Both officers Moerbauer and D'Hooge say that the OTP representatives were at police headquarters on 18th March 1996 from about 5.00 pm until 7.30 pm. On page 3560, beginning at line 10, Officer Moerbauer says this: "Question: Mr. Moerbauer, did you see on that same day of March 18th any investigator or any officer of ICTY? Answer: Yes, there were people from the Tribunal who were -- Question: Where? Answer: In the office in room 331." Further down on page 3560, line 24: "Question: I did not get you exactly. At what time did they arrive in room 331? Answer: Between 5.00 and 7.30. They were present during that time." On page 3976 of the transcript, Officer D'Hooge describes how the allegedly seized objects were placed on different tables and desks in room 331 how he and the OTP interpreter flipped through them and requested that certain documents be photocopied. Officer D'Hooge places himself in room 331 because that is the same room in which Mr. Mucic was located. Officer Moerbauer testified he made photocopies of documents selected by the OTP representatives immediately; that is to say some time between 5.00 pm and 7.30 pm on 18th March 1996. At page 3563, Officer Moerbauer says this: "Question: Mr. Moerbauer, my question was, did this request concern a selected number of documents? Answer: Well, the interpreter flipped through the folders and wanted to have copies of certain documents. Question: Approximately how many? Answer: Well, about 30 to 50 pages." Your Honours, it is at this point that what up until now has been consistent testimony between officers Moerbauer and D'Hooge changes. Officer Moerbauer says that the access by the representatives of the OTP to the allegedly seized material and the photocopies he made for them on the evening of 18th March 1996 between 5.00 pm and 7.30 had been approved by the investigating magistrate, Dr. Seda. During his testimony, Officer Moerbauer also told your Honours that the copies he made for the OTP that day were taken away by the representatives of the OTP when they left police headquarters that evening. On both counts, Officer D'Hooge gave different testimony. Officer D'Hooge said that no copies were made for the OTP on that evening of 18th March 1996, and no documents were taken away that evening because Dr. Seda could not be contacted to give his approval. Let me remind your Honours of what Officer D'Hooge said during his testimony at page 4001: "Question: In room 331, there is no photocopying machine; is that right? Answer: That is not the reason why they were not photocopied while we were there. The members of the Vienna police wanted to have authorisation of Dr. Seda, if they could, for the copying of the documents. Question: Therefore while you were there between 5.00 and 7.30 pm on that day, no documents were photocopied because there was no authorisation from Dr. Seda; is that correct? Answer: That is correct." Further down on page 4001, line 22, Officer D'Hooge says this: "Question: Do you know at all when these documents were photocopied? Answer: I believe that they were photocopied the moment that the Vienna police had authorisation from Dr. Seda and I believe that they could not get authorisation the same day because it was after working hours and probably Dr. Seda was not in his office any more." Officer Moerbauer has a different recollection of events. He says that the OTP representatives left on the evening of 18th March 1996 at about 7.30 with the documents he had photocopied for them. Moerbauer told this Tribunal on page 3565, line 10: "Question: When did you give the ICTY officers their copies? Answer: Well, all was done right away. I got a folder, made copies, went back and gave the copies to the person in question." Further down on page 3565 at line 19: "Question: What did you personally do after these photocopying operations? Answer: After the copies were finished the people from the Tribunal left. Question: On 18th March was there permission from the investigating magistrate Dr. Seda to allow officers from the OTP to have access to the allegedly seized items, to examine and handle them, to select items for photocopying, to receive documents from the Viennese police and to leave police headquarters with those items?" As I have just indicated to your Honours, Officer D'Hooge says that there was not. Officer D'Hooge says permission was only given by Dr. Seda on 20th March 1996 and this is at page 3997. In fact, under cross-examination, when pressed about the dates that Dr. Seda may have approved for the copies, Officer Moerbauer recalls that perhaps it was 20th March 1996 that such approval was obtained. At page 3716, Moerbauer says this: "Question: You, Mr. Moerbauer, never saw a document containing the approval of the magistrate judge, investigating judge for such an operation? Answer: There was no document, but notes were made regarding this. This was on the 18th or maybe on the latest the 20th. Mr. Bychek consulted the judge at that time and this was confirmed by the judge and a note on the record was made." Your Honours, the events to which Officer Moerbauer makes reference involving his colleague Bychek involves the handing over of four video cassettes allegedly seized from Door 10, which did occur on 20th March. Officer Moerbauer describes these events at page 3841. Moerbauer says: "It was on 20th March. Mr. Du Toit of the Tribunal was at our office and he was given the videotapes that had been seized. This was after consultation with Dr. Seda, the investigating judge and that consultation took place by calling Bychek over the phone. Mr. Du Toit also spoke via the telephone with Dr. Seda. Bychek wanted a written confirmation about the conversation with the investigating judge. The latter declined for reasons of time and in this regard, Mr. Bychek drew up a note.
